The rail connector of all France, under Paris

Hexagone3

A connector for every region of France. Three through stations under Paris, joined by three tunnels, link every line to every other, with the regular, reliable timetable that made the Swiss railways a model. And the capital gets a rare chance: four great parks, freed land and quicker journeys.

The idea

From four dead ends to one triangle

Today: every train stops at the end of the line

Four high-speed terminals, one for each direction. Trains come in, wait, and go back out the way they came. To go on, you take the metro across Paris to another station.

  • 118 platform tracks at the four terminals, and still full in the busy hours
  • Track fields that cut the north, the east and the south of Paris

The TGV triangle

Gare du Nord and Gare de l'Est merge into one deep station, Paris Nord-Est. With Gare de Lyon and Montparnasse, three through stations are joined by one twin-track tunnel on each side of the triangle.

  • 6 minutes from any station to any other
  • Every station has direct trains to every direction: north, east, south-east and Atlantic
  • No train reverses: each one stops twice and goes on

With TER and Transilien

Regional express trains (TER) run in the TGV tunnels, in the gaps between the TGVs, and on to the other side of the country. The suburban Transilien lines become new RER lines, crossing Paris instead of ending there.

  • G RER G: today's lines P and N merge into one line, from the north and the east through Nord-Est to Montparnasse
  • F RER F: today's lines L, H and K merge into one line, through Nord-Est and a deep Saint-Lazare to La Défense
  • The surface terminals close; their tracks become parks

The timetable

One beat of 12 minutes, the Swiss way

Every train stops 7 minutes, at the same minutes every hour, at all three stations. Here is why the beat is 12 minutes, and below, the busiest hour the stations can take.

7 min at the platform2 reserve3 to clear
12 minEach platform track takes a train every 12 minutes: 7 at the platform, then 2 kept free for a late train and 3 to clear the track. That makes 15 trains an hour on each side of each station.
6 minBetween any two of the stations the run is set at 6 minutes, half a beat, though 4.3 to 5.0 would do: trains run a little slower in the tunnels. A train that leaves one station on the beat reaches the next on the beat, so the three stations keep one clock.
Same minutes every hourA late train uses its 2 minutes of reserve or takes the next place of the beat. Everyone learns one pattern, and a small delay stays small instead of spreading through the station.

30 trains an hour at most in each tunnel and each direction, one every 2 minutes: the TGVs on the beat, the TER between them.

For all of France

Across France with no change in Paris

Today, crossing France by Paris means two changes: off the train, across the city by metro, onto another train, about 58 minutes in Paris. Only a few pairs of cities have direct trains, which go round Paris a few times a day. With the triangle every train runs through Paris: with the same number of trains as today, the direct links between the regions multiply, and every journey is shorter.

Times from SNCF's timetable for a weekday of March 2026, the connections a traveller would choose; the through train spends 20 minutes in Paris.2 Direct trains with the project: today's high-speed trains, each line keeping its count, run through and are shared between the other lines as in the timetable's hour; the trains round Paris keep running. Each change of train loses about 37% of travellers and today's journey by Paris has two, so direct trains bring many of them back. Only north to east keeps a change, on the same platforms at Paris Nord-Est.

Reaching the station

Two stations for every train, so one is nearer

Each train stops at two of the three stations. If you live in the south of Paris, your train to Lille now stops at Montparnasse or Gare de Lyon: no more trek to Gare du Nord. Every address in Paris is as close to its train as today or closer, up to 9.4 minutes closer; on average 27.4 minutes become 22.8.

Paris at the centre, for the whole country

Every main line of France leads to Paris, and today Paris is where they stop: a wall between the regions. Hexagone³ accepts that Paris is at the centre of the network and makes use of it. Through stations turn the dead ends into a crossroads, so the regions are joined to each other without depending on a change in the capital, and Paris gains parks, space and quicker trips at the same time.

Summary

Through stations under Paris

Every long-distance train to Paris ends in a dead-end station. This study tests replacing the four terminals used by high-speed trains by three deep through stations, Paris Nord-Est, Gare de Lyon and Montparnasse, joined in a triangle of high-speed tunnels. Regional express trains share the TGV tunnels, in the paths between the TGVs; RER G, a new line that joins today's suburban lines P and N, runs in its own tunnel from the north and east through Nord-Est to Montparnasse, and RER F, which joins today's lines H, K and L, from Nord-Est to a new deep station under Saint-Lazare. No train reverses, every station has direct trains to every direction, and nobody is further from a train than today. It would cost about €42 billion (€28 to 62 billion across unit prices and risk), and on the benefits counted it gives back more than it costs: 117% of its yearly cost each year, +€13.6bn in today's money under the French rules.

€42bnto build, with 15% for risk€28 to 62bn across the range of unit prices and of risk. 44.5 km of twin-track tunnel and 48 platform tracks in four deep stations
27.4 → 22.8minfrom a point in Paris to a station where the train stopsNo point is further than today. 23.2 min if the train's ride between its Paris stops is counted and the passenger picks a train that calls at their best station
189%of running costs coveredWith track charges on new TGV journeys, charges on new uses of the TGV and on regional express passengers, and half of the operators' saving on trainsets. 166% to 271% across the range of running costs; 164% with the charge on high-speed passengers alone
117%of the yearly cost returned in benefits+€13.6bn net in today's money under the French rules, 1.34 benefits to costs. Comparable tunnels were approved at 0.5 to 2 times their cost on their own basis, about 0.8 to 1.2 for the Elizabeth line on ours

The findings

The layout

Regional express trains in the TGV tunnels, a tunnel for each suburban line. TGVs keep their triangle: one tunnel on each side, 26.8 km with the approaches. Regional express trains run in the same tunnels, in the paths between the TGVs, which needs signalling for trains about 1.5 minutes apart: from the north through Nord-Est to Montparnasse and the Atlantic lines, from the east and from Gare de Lyon through Nord-Est to each other, so that none turns back. RER G, formed from today's lines P and N (11.5 km), runs from the north and east through Nord-Est to Montparnasse. RER F, formed from today's lines H, K and L (6.2 km), runs through Nord-Est to a new deep station under Saint-Lazare. The aim of the suburban lines is not the terminals but the jobs beyond them: RER G joins the north-east and east to the research and business clusters of the south-west (Massy, Saclay, Versailles, Saint-Quentin), RER F joins the northern suburbs without a change to Clichy-Levallois, Courbevoie and La Défense, and relieves RER E. Because every line at Gare du Nord and Gare de l'Est goes underground, their surface tracks are freed entirely for parks. At Gare de Lyon TGVs and regional express trains go underground, which frees the Bercy regional station too; line R keeps a few surface tracks. In all 48 platform tracks: 20 at Nord-Est, 14 at Montparnasse, 8 at Gare de Lyon, 6 at Saint-Lazare.

Passengers

Reaching a train gets quicker everywhere in Paris. Every station has direct trains to every direction, so the average time to a station where your train stops falls from 27.4 to 22.8 minutes at the door, 23.2 once the train's ride between its Paris stops is counted. The stations stay where they are: no point loses.

Crossing Paris

5.2 million passengers a year stop changing stations by metro. A change that takes 57.5 minutes today becomes a direct train or a change of platform: Atlantic to south-east in 20 minutes in Paris by the link, no reversal. Regional trains run on to a second station: lines H, K and L meet as RER F at Nord-Est and Saint-Lazare, P and N as RER G at Nord-Est and Montparnasse, regional express trains from the north at Montparnasse and those from the east at Gare de Lyon.

Cost

€41.7 billion, with 15% for risk on top of unit prices that already hold past overruns, because no station has been designed. Stations, €15.3 billion, and tunnels, €7.8 billion, are the two largest items of the €28.5 billion of works.

Traffic

+13.1 million high-speed and +31.1 million regional journeys a year. Most of the high-speed gain is between cities on two lines, which today need two or three changes in Paris: their traffic grows 3.0 times. The charge falls only on new uses, so no journey is lost. Passengers who go round Paris or avoid the train, and traffic growth, are not yet sized: they are study points.

Financing

Operations pay for themselves; construction cannot be repaid. Track charges on the new journeys, charges on new uses of the TGV and on regional express passengers, and half of the trainset saving cover 189% of running costs, and the surplus goes to construction. No land is sold. Construction needs a grant of €12 billion, 29% of the cost, on top of a business tax package: public money in all is about 81% of the cost.

Economic return

Benefits counted: €2.57 billion a year, 117% of the yearly cost; under the French rules, with growth, +€13.6bn net in today's money, paid back in 2072. Public budgets get back about €416 million a year in taxes. Passengers' time is nearly half of the benefits; the parks, the cross-France journeys and the regular timetable are counted, room for more trains only in the official reading.

The two accounts at a glance

What this means

As counted here, operations pay for themselves with a surplus, but construction is a public investment paid by taxes and grants for 81% of its cost: a grant of €12 billion on top of a new tax on businesses. Counted benefits return 117% of the yearly cost, in the range of comparable tunnels, and the official French reading, which lets traffic and the value of time grow, gives +€13.6bn net in today's money, paid back in 2072. That is a case for studying, not yet for building: the count rests on prices and running costs taken from few records, on a crossing traffic counted from the changes of vehicle removed, and on three assumptions with ranges, the room for more trains, the regular timetable and the later arrival at through platforms; the uncertain items together take the net value from +€4.4bn to +€25.2bn.

Six investigations would move the answer most: what limits the number of trains today; a fresh count of the passengers who cross Paris; the running costs net of what today's terminals cost; the region's travel model, to confirm the job access measured on the census; a survey of the track fields, for the parks; and the view of the railway on the regular timetable and the departure margin. They are listed in what to verify. Gare de Lyon's regional express trains, Bercy's included, now run underground through to Nord-Est. Only line R stays on the surface: running it through to an eastern line would cost about €2.1 billion more for 5 trains an hour with no proven partner, and is left as a later option.

How to use this document

The chapters follow the argument: the problem, what would be built, how it would run, what passengers gain, what it costs, who pays, what the country gets back, what could change the answer. Each can be read alone. Blue links with an arrow jump to the place where a point is treated; small numbers open the source.

Most figures can be explored: move a price in the cost chapter, a charge or a tax in the financing calculator, tap a point on the access map, pair two lines in crossing Paris, step through the works in the timeline.

Words used throughout. TGV: the French high-speed train. RER: the express suburban lines that already cross Paris underground. The link: the direct tunnel between the city ends of Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon, about 5 km assumption, which lets a train from the Atlantic run on to the south-east without passing through Nord-Est.

Three annexes explain the precedents the project draws on: how Zürich turned a terminus into a through station under a working hall, what the Elizabeth line changed in London and how it was paid for, and how the Swiss timetable makes every train meet every train.

Every number comes from a small model described in method and assumptions, or from a document listed in the sources. Assumptions are marked assumption, drawings that are not designs illustrative sketch. No station has been designed; this is a first test of whether the idea is worth a study.

Chapter 1

Why Paris stops every train

Every long-distance line into Paris ends at a buffer stop, in one of four separate stations. So every train has to turn round, a passenger crossing France has to cross the city by metro, and the busiest stations are short of room for more trains. Other cities have removed the same problem by running trains through.

Four stations, four dead ends

4terminals for high-speed trainsGare du Nord, Gare de l'Est, Gare de Lyon and Montparnasse. Inside Paris, no track joins one to another for long-distance trains
118platform tracks in the fourRER platforms included. Derived from published track lists, partly unverified3
5.2millionpassengers a year change station in ParisDerived from the last survey, in 2012-13, which counted 13,000 a day in the region4
57.5minfrom train to trainTaken in this study for a change of station today assumption The range assumed is 45 to 70 minutes

High-speed trains (TGV) from the north arrive at Gare du Nord, from the east at Gare de l'Est, from the south-east at Gare de Lyon and from the Atlantic coast at Montparnasse. Suburban and regional trains end at the same four stations, and the suburban lines of the west at a fifth, Saint-Lazare.

All four are terminals: the track stops at the end of the platform, and a train can only leave the way it came. A through station is the opposite: trains arrive at one end and leave by the other, without turning back.

Three things follow from the dead ends. A train holds its platform for a long time while it turns round. A traveller whose trip continues beyond Paris has to change station. And each line reaches only one corner of the city. The rest of this chapter takes them in turn.

Words used in this report
  • TGV: the French high-speed train. A full train is 400 m long; two coupled sets carry more than 1,000 passengers.
  • RER: the five express lines, A to E, that already cross Paris underground. Suburban lines H, K, P, N, R and L do not: they end at the terminals, L at Saint-Lazare. In this study's plan, P and N become one new RER line, called RER G, and H, K and L another, called RER F.
  • Regional express: trains from towns 50 to 250 km away (TER and Intercités), which also end at the terminals.
  • Hall: the large room of a station where passengers wait before going to the platforms.

A terminal uses its platforms badly, and the big ones are short of room

A train that arrives at a terminal is emptied, checked, often cleaned and restocked, filled again, and sent back out across the tracks it came in on. At Montparnasse the nine tracks kept for high-speed trains give at most nine departures an hour: one train per track per hour.6 A TGV that only stops needs 3 minutes, or 4 to 5 at the largest stations.7 Through stations are planned for four to six long-distance trains an hour on each platform track: Stuttgart's new station, not yet open, reached about six in a simulated stress test.8 9 One that is in service, Zürich's Löwenstrasse station, handles about 460 trains a day on four tracks, about six an hour on each on average,10 though the through trains that wait for connections there stand 6 to 9 minutes (derived from the departure boards; see Zürich).11 12

The rule this study uses for its own stations. Platforms are dedicated by direction, 3 tracks each way at each station. A stop takes 7 minutes; the track is then held 2 minutes more for a late train, and after the departure it needs about 3 minutes before the next train can arrive. So each train takes a place of 12 minutes and one track takes 5 trains an hour assumption, all three figures, as in the timetable. Three tracks each way take 15 trains an hour, about the most a high-speed line brings, 15 to 16. What limits the number of trains today, the platforms or the lines outside Paris, is a study point (I1 in what to verify). How the rule sizes the new stations is in how many platforms.

  • Gare du Nord was turned down as the terminal of the airport express for lack of capacity.15 It already handles 2,200 trains and 700,000 passengers a day.16
  • Gare de Lyon must find room. The high-speed line to Lyon is being upgraded from 13 to 16 trains an hour each way by 2030, and the station has to take them.17
  • The tracks cut the city. Approach tracks and platforms run from each terminal out to the ring road and divide the neighbourhoods on both sides. Freeing them for parks means taking every line underground: at Gare du Nord and Gare de l'Est, one line left on the surface would keep its tracks across the site and lose most of the gain. What the project would free is in changes to today's stations.

Crossing France means crossing Paris by metro

A traveller from Lille to Lyon gets off at Gare du Nord, takes the RER or the metro to Gare de Lyon and boards a second train. The last survey, in 2012-13, counted 13,000 passengers a day changing between two stations in the region.4 Scaled by the growth of high-speed traffic since, that is about 5.2 million a year (derived; no newer count is published). With the stations joined, the same traveller stays on the train, or changes on the platforms of one station.

Some trains already go round Paris. The bypass line east of the city, opened in 1994 to 1996, carries trains from one region to another without entering Paris, with stops at Marne-la-Vallée, Roissy and Massy. They carried 21.9 million passengers in 2009, 17.6 million of them on trains through those outer stations.18 For the pairs that include the Atlantic line they are slow and few: Bordeaux to Lille takes 5h05 on the few direct trains round Paris and 4h27 with a change of station in Paris, against 3h39 through Paris (SNCF's timetable for a weekday of March 2026, the connections a traveller would choose; the through train spends 20 minutes in Paris).2 assumption. The passengers these trains do not carry, by car, by air or not travelling, are not in the count above; crossing Paris by TGV comes back to them.

The seats are short where the gain is largest. On the Atlantic line a new operator, Velvet, has ordered 12 trains to run between Paris and Bordeaux, Nantes, Rennes and Angers from 2028, and says it will add 10 million seats a year to a market where, by its own account, 15% of would-be rail passengers go by car, coach or air for want of trains.19 The line to Lyon is being upgraded from 13 to 16 trains an hour each way by 2030.17 Demand is there; the terminals are where it meets its limit.

Two other groups of passengers pay for the dead ends.

  • Each traveller has one station to go to. A Parisian leaving for Bordeaux must reach Montparnasse, wherever in the city the trip starts. From the north-east of Paris that is a long metro ride with changes. Reaching the station measures it.
  • Suburban lines stop at the edge of the centre. Lines H, K, P, N, R and L each end at a terminal. A commuter from the northern suburbs who works at La Défense changes at Gare du Nord to RER E, which the plan describes as saturated in the morning; one from the north-east who works on the research and business campuses of the south-west, Massy, Saclay, Versailles or Saint-Quentin, changes twice. The plan's reading is that trips from suburb to suburb across Paris are few today because they are so hard to make, not for want of demand, the reasoning on which the Grand Paris Express ring, line 15, was built. Regional and suburban passengers gives the numbers.
  • What the through lines are for. The plan runs RER G (today's lines P and N) from the east through Nord-Est to Montparnasse and the south-west, and RER F (today's lines H, K and L) from the north through Nord-Est to a new deep station under Saint-Lazare and on to Clichy-Levallois, Courbevoie and La Défense. Their point is less the second terminal than the job areas beyond it: two employment corridors across Paris, and RER F relieves RER E. RER F also joins Saint-Lazare and the western suburbs directly to Gare du Nord, for line K, RER B and the airport. Regional express trains run through as well, in the paths between the TGVs in the TGV tunnels: those from the north on to Montparnasse and the Atlantic lines, those from the east on to Gare de Lyon and Burgundy. The benefits of these corridors are measured on the census commuting flows in the economic return; the region's travel model would confirm them (a study point in what to verify).
Other cities have done it

Zürich put four through tracks under its terminal, Vienna replaced two terminals with one through station, and Stuttgart is replacing 16 terminal platforms with 8 through tracks.10 20 8 Paris itself did it for part of its suburban network with the RER. The annexes on Zürich and London give the record of two of them, and the next chapter describes what would be built in Paris.

Chapter 2

What would be built

Three deep TGV stations under the existing ones, joined in a triangle, and a fourth deep station under Saint-Lazare for RER F, a new line that joins today’s suburban lines H, K and L. TGVs, RER G (today’s lines P and N, joined) and RER F each have their own tunnel, and the regional express trains share the TGV tunnels: 44.5 km of twin-track tunnel in all, so that every train of Gare du Nord, Gare de l’Est and Montparnasse, and every regional express train of Gare de Lyon, can leave the surface and their tracks can become parks. Every TGV stops at two of the three stations, and each of the three has direct TGVs to all four directions. Nothing here has been designed: the map and the quantities are planning assumptions.

Four deep stations and three kinds of tunnel

4deep through stationsParis Nord-Est, Gare de Lyon, Montparnasse and Saint-Lazare: 48 platform tracks, 20, 8, 14 and 6
44.5kmof twin-track tunnel26.8 km TGV (with the 5 km link), also used by the regional express trains, 11.5 km RER G, 6.2 km RER F
15.3kmof platform track400 m long for TGVs, 350 m for regional express trains, 225 m for suburban trains
4station halls kept, parks in place of the tracksThe listed halls of Gare du Nord, Gare de l’Est and Gare de Lyon, and the recent hall of Montparnasse, become the entrances to the stations below. Most of the surface tracks become parks; line R keeps a small surface terminal at Gare de Lyon

A through station is a station where trains arrive at one end and leave by the other, without turning back. A twin-track tunnel carries two tracks, one each way. A corridor is a route followed by one or more such tunnels side by side. A portal is the place where a tunnel comes up to join an existing line. An underground junction is a cavern where two tunnels become one. The TGV is the French high-speed train. Regional express trains are the TER services that join Paris to the towns of the surrounding regions. The RER is the set of express suburban lines that cross Paris underground, A to E today. The project adds two: RER F joins today’s suburban lines H, K and L into one line, and RER G joins today’s lines P and N.

The approach corridors run from each station to the existing tracks at the ring road, where the tunnels come up; on the eastern line they come up at Rosa Parks, just inside it, and RER F comes up near Pont-Cardinet, on the tracks out of Saint-Lazare. A tunnel 35 to 40 m deep needs only about 1.1 to 1.2 km to reach the surface, and a kilometre kept underground costs far more than a kilometre of existing track, so the tunnels go no further. The three TGV stations form a triangle: two sides of it run through Paris Nord-Est, the third is the direct link between the two southern stations. Switch each kind of tunnel, and the regional express trains in the TGV tunnels, on and off, and select a station, a corridor, a portal or a junction to read its facts.

Separation by type of train

TGVs, RER G and RER F each have their own twin-track tunnel, as the plan sets out; the regional express trains run in the TGV tunnels, between the TGVs. There is one TGV tunnel on each side of the triangle: Nord-Est to Gare de Lyon, Nord-Est to Montparnasse, and the direct link between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon, with the four TGV approaches from the north, the east, the south-east and the Atlantic. Between Nord-Est and Montparnasse, two tunnels run side by side: the TGV tunnel, which the regional express trains share, and RER G. Between Nord-Est and Gare de Lyon there is only the TGV tunnel, shared in the same way. RER F has a tunnel of its own, from the north under Nord-Est to a new deep station under Saint-Lazare, and back up onto the tracks at Pont-Cardinet.

Nord-Est to Montparnasse, seen in cross-section

Cross-section of the corridor, not to scale illustrative sketch. Whether two tunnels fit side by side, under the Seine, has not been studied. On the RER E extension opened in 2024, one tunnel 9.6 m wide inside carries two tracks.21

What runs in each tunnel

  • TGV, 26.8 km: all the high-speed trains, on the triangle and the four approaches. The link exists for the 9 TGVs an hour each way between the Atlantic and the south-east when both lines are full.
  • Regional express trains, in the TGV tunnels: at the peak, the 11 an hour each way of the north run through Nord-Est to Montparnasse and on to the Chartres, Le Mans and Granville lines, so the Atlantic side goes from 7 to 11; the 3 of the east, and 1 new hourly train, run through Nord-Est to Gare de Lyon and on to Burgundy. No regional express train turns back in Paris, and the Bercy station is freed. They have platforms of their own at Nord-Est, Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon, but no tunnel of their own.
  • RER G, 11.5 km: today’s suburban lines P (east) and N (south-west) become one line, called RER G, through Nord-Est and Montparnasse.
  • RER F, 6.2 km: today’s suburban lines H and K (north) and L (west) become one line, called RER F; the branches of line L become further branches of RER F. The ride from Nord-Est to Saint-Lazare takes 4 minutes.
  • What it adds up to. 44.5 km of twin-track tunnel, 8 portals and 4 junction caverns.

Sharing the TGV tunnels: paths every 2 minutes

A path is a slot in the timetable for one train through a tunnel. In the TGV tunnels the paths are 2 minutes apart, 30 an hour each way. The TGVs keep their places of the 12-minute beat, and the regional express trains take the paths in between. TGV times shown to passengers do not change: the 2-minute reserve in the beat becomes the window between the doors closing, the public departure time, and the train leaving. Every train, TGV or regional, takes the same 6-minute run between stations, so none catches up with another. Which trains use which paths is in trains and timetable.

The condition: signalling for trains 1.5 minutes apart

Sharing works only if trains can follow each other about 1.5 minutes apart in the tunnels: ETCS level 2, the European cab signalling by radio, with short blocks and automatic driving in the tunnels assumption. The usual rule (UIC 406) keeps a line under 75% of its capacity at the peak. With trains 1.5 minutes apart, the busiest tunnel, the Atlantic approach, is at 65%; if the signalling only reached 2 minutes it would be at 87%, and the regional express trains would need a tunnel of their own from Montparnasse to Vanves, 2.8 km, about €0.9 billion all-in. That option is noted, not built.

The tighter limit is not in the tunnels but at the platforms: the 4 regional express tracks of Nord-Est are occupied 105 of 120 minutes an hour each way (88%), those of Montparnasse 64%, and the fourth track each way at Gare de Lyon 40 of 60 minutes (67%). None has been drawn as a full timetable.

Why these through lines

Separating the kinds of train keeps each tunnel simple: a late suburban train never holds up a TGV, and each suburban tunnel can be signalled like a metro line. The regional express trains are the exception: they share the TGV paths, so a late one can hold up a TGV, and their timekeeping matters as much as the TGVs’ own assumption. But the through lines were chosen for where they lead, not for the Paris stations themselves; this is the plan’s reasoning.

  • RER G is an employment corridor. The point is not that line P riders reach Montparnasse: they have other ways. Today’s line N serves the research, science, university and company clusters of the south-west, at Massy-Palaiseau, Polytechnique, Saclay, Versailles and Saint-Quentin. Joining it to line P puts the homes of the north-east and the east much closer to those highly qualified jobs.
  • RER F leads to La Défense. The point is not Saint-Lazare, which RER E already serves. It is a ride without a change from the northern suburbs to Pont-Cardinet, Clichy-Levallois, Courbevoie and La Défense, large job clusters, and it relieves RER E, which is saturated in the morning. It also joins Saint-Lazare and the western suburbs directly to Gare du Nord: the airport connections, line K, and an easy change to RER B towards Roissy, Villepinte and Tremblay-en-France.
  • Suburb to suburb. Trips from one side of the Paris region to the other are rare today because they are nearly impossible, not for lack of demand. Grand Paris Express line 15 was built on that same reasoning.
  • Everything underground at Nord and Est. Taking every line of Gare du Nord and Gare de l’Est underground frees all the surface tracks of both stations for the park; leaving even one line on the surface would keep most of the cost of the tracks and lose the park.

The regional benefit of the station model measures the minutes saved to reach Paris destinations near the second station; the employment corridors beyond the stations are measured on the census commuting flows in the economic return.

The platforms are sized by the plan’s rules assumption. Regional express: a 5-minute stop with margin and a 2-minute gap give 8 trains an hour a track, so 16 each way on the 4 tracks of Nord-Est, against 15 at the peak with the plan. Suburban: 10 trains an hour a track, so 20 each way for RER G (peak 11 on P and 12 on N, 16 with the Clamart plan) and 30 for RER F (peak 23 on H and K, 24 to 28 on L). None has been drawn as a timetable.

Gare de Lyon: line R stays on the surface. The regional express trains of Gare de Lyon and Bercy go underground on the 8 tracks of the new station and run through to Nord-Est, so Bercy is freed. Line R, a suburban line of Gare de Lyon, keeps a small terminal of a few surface tracks. Running it through as well, paired with extra line P trains towards Meaux or Provins, would need 2 more tracks at Gare de Lyon and 2 at Nord-Est, 330 m long, about €2.1 billion all-in, for 5 trains an hour with no proven demand for the pairing: it is left as a later option, the one open item at Gare de Lyon.

The cost is built up in the cost chapter; which trains use which tracks, and how the link is used, is in trains and timetable.

Left as it is

  • The five RER lines, A to E, which already cross Paris underground.
  • The metro.
  • The surface station of Saint-Lazare, for line J and the Normandy trains; Austerlitz station.

  • The train depots, which stay beside the approach lines; see changes at today's stations.

Not included in the cost

  • New trains.
  • Clearing the surface tracks once they are closed, and making the parks.
  • Anything built beside the parks.
  • Running line R through underground, a later option of about €2.1 billion.

How the stations sit under the present ones is in the stations. How all this could be built while trains keep running is in works and stages.

Parks where the tracks were

Once both stages are open, every train of Gare du Nord, Gare de l’Est and Montparnasse runs underground, and the fans of tracks inside Paris are no longer needed: the two fans north of Gare du Nord and Gare de l’Est, and the tracks from Montparnasse to the ring road. This is why every line of Nord and Est goes underground: leaving even one on the surface would keep the tracks and lose the park. At Gare de Lyon the TGVs and the regional express trains go underground and the Bercy station is freed; only line R keeps a small terminal and a few tracks, so most of the fan towards Bercy can become a park too. The project turns the freed tracks into parks, from the end of each station building outwards, with some small plots kept for new buildings or for reusing the buildings already there. About 160 hectares of track fields, an estimate read from maps assumption; about 109 are freed once the tracks the RER, line R and freight keep are taken out, 87 of them as parks and 16 as building plots. No official measure of the track corridors exists. The one published figure found is about 30 hectares of rail corridor inside the Bercy-Charenton development area (derived).25

What stays

  • The four halls, as entrances to the stations below.
  • The RER and metro stations under them.
  • The surface station of Saint-Lazare, for line J and the Normandy trains.
  • The depots, beyond the ring road, reached through the portals and the existing tracks.

What is not counted

  • No income from the land enters the accounts; the sale of the small plots is counted once in the economic return.
  • The parks are valued in the economic return, by the visits they draw and the health they bring, net of what they cost to clear, make and keep; their area is read from plans and never measured.
  • Clearing the tracks, making the parks and building on the small plots are not in the construction cost of the project; the economic return counts them against the parks and the plots.

Two points are open. The airport express train to Roissy is due to end at surface platforms of Gare de l’Est;15 what becomes of it, when all the surface tracks there are freed, has not been studied. And line R keeps a small surface terminal at Gare de Lyon; running it through later would free a little more land, at about €2.1 billion; see separation by type of train.

Chapter 3

How the stations would be laid out

Nobody has designed these stations: three TGV stations, at Paris Nord-Est, Gare de Lyon and Montparnasse, and a suburban station at Saint-Lazare. This chapter sketches where each would sit under the present station, what is already underground there, and how a passenger would get from the street down to the train. In the illustration used by the model, reaching a deep platform takes 4.0 minutes from the hall, against 3.7 minutes to walk down a terminal platform today. That near-equality rests on assumptions that a concept design must check.

Paris Nord-Est: one station under two halls

How to read the drawings

Every drawing in this chapter is an illustrative sketch. Only dimensions with a source, or taken from the model, are printed as numbers. Positions, shapes and the order of the platforms are invented to make the sketch readable. Dashed outlines mark structures whose depth is not published.

Gare du Nord and Gare de l’Est are 500 m apart; the walk between them takes 8 to 14 minutes today.5 Between the two, about 30 m down, lies Magenta, a station opened in 1999 on line E of the RER, the express suburban lines that cross Paris underground: 4 tracks in a cavern 225 m long and 54 m wide.24

The new station would be entered from either hall. It has 20 platform tracks: 6 for TGVs at 400 m, grouped three for trains towards the north and the east and three for trains towards the south, 4 for regional express trains at 350 m, 4 for RER G, the new suburban line that joins today’s lines P and N, and 6 for RER F, which joins today’s lines H, K and L, both at 225 m. Each kind of train has its own platforms. Regional express trains run in the TGV tunnels, in the paths between the TGVs (see the hour); RER G and RER F each have a tunnel of their own. All the platforms sit side by side in one box, the 4 regional express tracks on the west side. Northern regional trains leave the TGV tracks by plain turnouts; eastern ones, which run on to Gare de Lyon, cross the TGV lines by one dive-under at each end of the station assumption. Every train that uses Gare du Nord and Gare de l’Est today moves underground, so that all the surface tracks of both stations are freed: leaving even one line on the surface would keep most of the cost and lose the park. Once the surface tracks are cleared, the box can be dug in the open on the freed track field rather than mined under it assumption. The station is about 7 times the platform length of Magenta. Nothing of this size has been built under Paris. The deep through stations of Stuttgart and Berlin have 8 tracks each (Berlin unverified).8 26

What is not known. Whether 20 tracks fit on one level between the two halls, at what depth, and how they pass Magenta, the RER station of Gare du Nord and three metro lines. This station alone is carried at €8.8 billion with design, land and 15% risk, 21% of the whole project. A concept design of it is the first study to commission; see what to verify.

Gare de Lyon: beside a five-level RER station, near the Seine

Gare de Lyon has 22 surface tracks in two halls (unverified);32 the seven platforms of Hall 1 are already 400 m long.33 Its underground station is one of the largest in Paris: RER lines A and D on five levels, 315 m long and 41 m wide, with RER D above RER A (unverified).34 The RER D tunnel is 20 m deep.35 Metro line 14 runs beside it (unverified).36

The new station would have 8 platform tracks of 400 m, 4 each way. Three each way take the TGVs of the 12-minute beat. The fourth, one each way, takes the 16th TGV of the hour on the south-east line, which six tracks could not hold, and the 4 regional express trains (TER) an hour each way that run through from Paris Nord-Est to Burgundy: it is busy 40 of 60 minutes in the peak hour (67%). The TER share the TGV tunnel from Paris Nord-Est. All the TER of Gare de Lyon and of Bercy move underground and run through, so the TER tracks of Gare de Lyon and the Bercy station are freed. At its city end the TGV tracks fork: towards Paris Nord-Est, and towards the direct link to Montparnasse, 5 km long, which passes under the Seine. The natural place for the station is under today's surface platforms, beside the RER station. Neither the station nor the junction has been studied; the geometry of the link is a study point.

Suburban line R stays on the surface, on a small terminal of a few surface tracks. It is the one open item left at Gare de Lyon. R cannot simply use the two new tracks: the fourth track each way is already busy 40 of 60 minutes, and with the 5 trains an hour of line R it would need 70, more than one track can give. A through train must also run on, and at Paris Nord-Est the regional express tracks would go from 105 to 135 of 120 minutes. Running R through would therefore need 2 more tracks at Gare de Lyon and 2 at Paris Nord-Est, 330 m long, about €2.1 billion with all mark-ups. The south-east tunnel itself could take R: 25 trains an hour, 63% of its capacity with trains about 1.5 minutes apart, so no extra approach tunnel would be needed. Its partner beyond Paris Nord-Est would be extra trains on the branches of today's line P towards Meaux or Provins assumption. With no proven demand for those trains, this is left as a later option, for the growth that line R may see; it is not in the cost.

Montparnasse: under a station already covered by a slab

Montparnasse has 28 platform tracks, 24 in the main station and 4 at its Vaugirard annexe.6 The platforms are one level above the street: Hall 1 is on level 2.38 They are already covered by a slab that carries a garden of 3.5 hectares, the Jardin Atlantique (unverified).39 Four metro lines meet around the station (unverified).40

The new station would have 14 platform tracks: 6 for TGVs, three each way, 4 for regional express trains at 350 m and 4 for RER G at 225 m. They arrive from Paris Nord-Est in two tunnels side by side, one for TGVs, which the regional express trains share in the paths between the TGVs, and one for RER G, and leave on the Atlantic side: the regional express trains towards Chartres, Le Mans and Granville, RER G towards Versailles and the south-west. At its city end the TGV tracks fork towards Paris Nord-Est, under the Seine, and towards the direct link to Gare de Lyon, which also passes under the river. This part of Paris stands over old limestone quarries: 770 hectares of the city are undermined, in eight arrondissements that include the 14th and 15th, where the station stands.41

Saint-Lazare: a suburban through station under a working station

RER F, which joins today's lines H, K and L, runs in its own tunnel from the north, under Paris Nord-Est and on to a new deep through station under Saint-Lazare, 2.6 km from Nord-Est, a ride of 4 minutes. Beyond it the tracks climb back to the surface in 1.2 km and join the tracks of line L towards Pont-Cardinet, Clichy-Levallois, Courbevoie and La Défense, whose branches become further branches of RER F. The new station has 6 suburban platform tracks of 225 m. It has no TGV or regional express platforms.

Saint-Lazare has 27 platform tracks today (unverified).42 The surface station stays: line J and the trains to Normandy keep their tracks, and the station keeps working during the works. Close by, about 30 m down, lies Haussmann-Saint-Lazare, the twin of Magenta on RER line E: 4 tracks in a cavern 225 m long.24 Metro lines 3, 12, 13 and 14 meet at Saint-Lazare (unverified).43

Room for passengers: the halls once the trains are underground

Three of today's stations have a large covered hall at the street end: the historic halls of Gare du Nord and Gare de Lyon, and the covered platform level of Montparnasse. Each is about 150 m long. Passengers have about the first 30 m of it; the rest is taken by the ends of the tracks and their platforms (estimated from the SNCF station plans assumption). The waiting areas are crowded: Gare du Nord was designed for 500,000 passengers a day and takes more than 700,000;44 at Montparnasse the concourse across the platforms is largely taken up by people waiting.45

With the platforms deep underground, the whole of each hall becomes a hall for passengers: a place to wait, meet, eat and shop above the platforms, and the way down to them. At Gare de Lyon this is Hall 1. The tracks beyond the end of each building become parks; at Gare de Lyon a few surface tracks stay for the small terminal of line R (see the parks where the tracks were). Gare de l'Est, the second entrance to Nord-Est, keeps its halls as an entrance and is not counted here; nor is Saint-Lazare, whose surface station stays in use.

The mezzanine. Above the deep platforms, a hall runs across the station at each way down, as wide as the tracks: 270 m at Nord-Est for 20 tracks, 189 m at Montparnasse for 14 and 108 m at Gare de Lyon for 8, at the width per track of Magenta.24 Taken 30 m deep assumption, it is a second hall where passengers wait above their platform and where shops and cafés can be placed. Its cost is part of the station price per metre of platform (see the prices used).

What it could mean for shops. Montparnasse shows how much a station can hold when space is found: 19,000 m² for 86 million people a year, against 5,214 m² of sales area at Gare du Nord for 292 million (lettable area is larger than sales area, so the two are not quite comparable). The income counted in the operations account takes shops in the new halls only; more shops in the freed historic halls are not counted. The halls have not been designed: how much becomes shops and how much waiting space is to be studied.

How deep, and why

The new platforms have to pass under what is already there: metro lines, RER stations, sewers and the foundations of buildings. At Paris Nord-Est, Magenta is already 30 m down. The model's illustration takes 35 m for all four stations assumption. That is within the range of stations that have been built, but it is not a design depth.

Depth does not strain the approaches. European rules allow tracks to slope by up to 35 mm per metre.22 A tunnel can therefore gain or lose 35 m of depth in one kilometre (derived). Platforms 35 to 40 m deep therefore need only about 1.1 to 1.2 km of tunnel to reach the surface. The portals are 2.4 to 2.9 km from the stations, on the existing tracks at the ring road (at Rosa Parks for the eastern line), which leaves room for the climb beyond the junctions; the TGV stations are 5 to 6 km from each other through Paris Nord-Est, and the direct link between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon is 5 km. RER F is the tight case: its tracks come back up 1.2 km west of Saint-Lazare, room for a climb of about 42 m at the steepest slope (derived). The link does not change the argument: even at a steady 35 m, it has room to dip under the Seine and come back.

The Seine is crossed in two places, between Paris Nord-Est and Montparnasse, where two tunnels pass under it side by side (TGV, which the regional express trains share, and RER G), and on the link between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon, a TGV tunnel only. RER F stays on the right bank. Gare du Nord, Gare de l’Est and Gare de Lyon are all on the right bank; Montparnasse is on the left. Two lines already pass under the river in the centre: RER line B, on a ramp of 4%, and metro line 14 (unverified).57 37

From the hall to the coach

Deep platforms are further from the street than surface ones. But a terminal has its own long walk: the train stands beyond the gates, and the average coach is 200 m down the platform. A through station is entered from above, at several points along its length. Follow a passenger through both.

With platforms 35 m down, the deep station comes out at 4.0 minutes and the terminal at 3.7 minutes. The difference, about 18 seconds, is well inside the uncertainty of such a sketch. The figures are the same at the three TGV stations: Gare de Lyon and Montparnasse have fewer tracks than Paris Nord-Est, which makes them narrower, not shorter, and a TGV platform is 400 m long at each. On a regional express platform of 350 m the average coach is about 44 m from a way down instead of 50, and on a suburban platform of 225 m, at Saint-Lazare for instance, about 28 m (derived). No measured times are published for the Paris terminals or for deep stations. The State's regional travel model applies a penalty to deep stations; its value is not published.59

What the model does with this

The central case takes the time inside the station as equal to today's. That is an assumption, and the result is sensitive to it: the sensitivity tests include two minutes more for every passenger, which removes 30% of the benefits.

Time inside the station is a separate matter from the time to reach its door. How long it takes to get from home or work to the entrance of a station where one's train stops is measured in reaching the station. The minutes on this page come on top, in both the present stations and the new ones.

How the station is run matters as much as how deep it is:

  • Today the platform is shown about 20 minutes before departure, and the gates close 2 minutes before.60 The passengers of a whole train, more than 1,000 when two sets are coupled, cross the hall in the same few minutes. SNCF tested showing platforms 30 minutes ahead in 2018.61
  • With fixed platforms, nobody waits for a screen. Passengers go down when they arrive and wait at the mark for their coach, as on Swiss platforms.62
  • Platforms by direction make the way down simpler. Every train for the south leaves from one of the same three platforms, so a passenger for Lyon or Marseille heads for the same part of the station every time, and the passage above the platforms needs fewer branches.
  • Two stops spread the crowd. The passengers of one train board at two stations, so each platform handles fewer people for each train.
  • The halls become waiting rooms. British design rules size a hall for the whole flow of the busiest quarter of an hour when the platform is announced late, and for a tenth of it when the platform is known in advance.58
  • London trains board differently. Their passengers pass the border checks in a control hall of their own and board from a platform closed off for the time of the stop, as described for Paris Nord-Est.

A benefit that is not counted: for trains that run every two hours or less often, the official method adds a 20-minute margin before departure.63 If fixed platforms let long-distance passengers arrive 5 minutes later, that would be worth about €223 million a year. No measurement exists of how early French passengers reach the station, so this stays out of the totals.

Chapter 4

Works, changes to today's stations, and stages

The stations would be built under five terminals that stay in use, and 44.5 km of tunnel under the city. This chapter shows how such works have been done elsewhere, what would change at each of today's stations, and how the project could open in two stages. The model assumes 12 years of works. That is an assumption, not a programme: there is no design and no ground investigation.

Four ways of building, all used before

Little can be dug from the street: the stations lie under working stations and the tunnels under buildings. Four methods have been used for works of this kind, in Paris or under a working terminal. Which one would serve where has not been studied.

1. A cavern dug from below

Workers reach the level of the station through a shaft, then dig the cavern from inside, a section at a time, and line it with concrete. Nothing is opened at the surface but the shafts.

  • Paris, Magenta and Haussmann-Saint-Lazare, 1999. Two stations of the RER, the express suburban lines that cross Paris underground. Each is a central vault with two side vaults, 54 m and 58 m wide for four tracks, about 30 m down.24
  • At Magenta the ground was first strengthened with 3,570 columns of injected cement, and it still gave way once during the works.24
  • The line ended 44% above its approved cost. The review names the complexity of the project and the hazards of underground work.64

2. A box built from the top down, under working tracks

Walls are sunk from the surface and a roof is cast between them. Trains run again on the roof while the station is dug out underneath.

  • Zürich, Löwenstrasse, 2014. Four tracks 16 m under the terminal tracks,10 built between September 2007 and June 2014.65 10
  • Two or three tracks at a time, normally two, were shortened by 100 m; trains ran on all the others.66 67 Part of the roof and walls had been built in advance, when the platforms above were rebuilt.68
  • Under a listed wing of the station, 110 m were dug beneath the standing building; it settled 10 to 15 mm, with 25 mm allowed.69 See the Zürich annex.
  • Paris, Porte Maillot, 2024. Where nothing stands above, the box is simply dug open: 35 m deep, in 32 months.55

3. A station under a standing building

The building is first carried on new foundations. The station is then dug underneath it.

  • Paris, La Défense, 2024. The RER E station lies under an exhibition hall. Of the hall's 253 columns, 118 were moved onto about 1,800 small piles and a slab 3 m thick.70
  • The contract ran for 61 months.71 This station was under-estimated by €100 million, one of the named causes of the 45% overrun of the extension.72

4. Tunnels bored by machine

A cutting head as wide as the tunnel is lowered down a shaft. It digs forward and lines the tunnel with concrete rings behind it.

  • Paris, RER E extension, 2024. 8 km of tunnel 30 to 40 m deep, of which about 6 km in one tube 9.6 m wide inside for two tracks, with 10 shafts for air and rescue.21
  • London, Elizabeth line. Eight machines bored 42 km of tunnel between May 2012 and May 2015.73
  • Here: 44.5 km of twin-track tunnel: 26.8 km for TGVs, the 5 km link between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon included, which the regional express trains share, 11.5 km for RER G, the line joining today’s lines P and N, and 6.2 km for RER F, the line joining today’s lines H, K and L.

Method drawings illustrative sketch, not to scale.

The link and its two junctions. The link itself, 5 km under the city and the Seine, would most likely be bored by machine, like the other tunnels. Its two junction caverns, where the link leaves the corridor from Nord-Est at the city end of each southern station, are a different matter: a cavern widening under a working station, dug from below or from the station box, with the ground and the groundwater of each site unknown. Which method they would need is not known, and the geometry of the link is a study point. Each junction cavern is carried at €250 million of works assumption. There are 4 in all, all on the TGV tunnels: these two, and the two on either side of Paris Nord-Est where the tunnels from the north and the east meet and where those to Gare de Lyon and Montparnasse part. The regional express trains have no tunnel and no junction of their own.

Two tunnels side by side. Between Paris Nord-Est and Montparnasse, 6 km under the city and the Seine, the TGV tunnel, which the regional express trains share, and the RER G tunnel run side by side. Each would be bored as its own drive, from shared shafts and work sites, so that one corridor of work sites serves both assumption. The two cross under the Seine together; where, and at what depth, is not known. Elsewhere a corridor carries one or two tunnels: the north carries the TGV and RER F tunnels, the east the TGV and RER G tunnels.

Portals. The tunnels come up through 8 portals onto existing tracks: 4 for the TGV tunnels, 2 for RER G (east and Atlantic) and 2 for RER F (north, and west of Saint-Lazare towards Pont-Cardinet).

Ways in for the regional express trains. With no tunnel of their own, the regional express trains need links onto the TGV tracks: tie-ins at both ends of their platforms at Nord-Est and at Montparnasse, two dive-unders in the Nord-Est throats where the eastern trains cross under the TGV lines, and links at three TGV portal ramps, north, east and Atlantic. They are costed together at €0.65 billion of works assumption; their design, like that of the junctions, is a study point.

Saint-Lazare, under a working station. The RER F station is dug under a terminal that stays open throughout: Saint-Lazare keeps its surface station for line J and the trains to Normandy, during the works and after. Haussmann-Saint-Lazare, the RER E station close by, was dug in the 1990s as a cavern from below, the first method above.24 How the new station would be dug, and how many platforms above could be spared in turn, has not been studied.

None of these has been done at this size

The Paris caverns have four tracks and the Zürich box four; the deep through stations of Stuttgart and Berlin have eight.8 26 Paris Nord-Est would have 20, under two terminals at once, Montparnasse 14, Gare de Lyon 8 and Saint-Lazare 6, under a station that stays open. The price of that step is the largest unknown in the cost.

No official measure of the four track corridors exists; the one published figure found is about 30 hectares of rail corridor inside the Bercy-Charenton development area (derived).25 The land is not sold in the accounts; the parks are valued by their visits and the health they bring in the economic return, net of clearing and making them, and the small plots kept for building are counted sold once. Their area is a study point. See the parks where the tracks were.
  • Depots stay where they are, beside the approach lines, and trains reach them through the portals. The depots of the TGV, the French high-speed train, are at Le Landy, 2 km north of Gare du Nord (unverified),74 at Pantin and Bobigny for the eastern line (unverified),75 and at Châtillon for the Atlantic line.6 Those of the south-eastern line were not located in the sources found. The cost includes €0.6 billion for sidings and links to the depots assumption.
  • London trains get no track of their own. For each departure one of the six TGV tracks at Paris Nord-Est is closed off for the time of the stop; the border checks are made in a control hall and waiting room on the Gare du Nord side, and boarding takes 10 to 15 minutes assumption, as Amsterdam does from one closed-off platform.28 Trains from London are checked before departure and run on to the south. See the Nord-Est station.
  • Two questions left open. The airport express train to Roissy is due to end at surface platforms of Gare de l’Est.15 What becomes of it has not been studied. And line R keeps a small surface terminal at Gare de Lyon: running it through underground, with 2 more tracks at Gare de Lyon and 2 at Nord-Est, is a later option of about €2.1 billion, not in the cost; see the networks in the tunnels.

Building in two stages

The project divides into two parts that can open one after the other. The costs below are with design, land and 15% risk. Whether to build in stages at all, and in this order, is a study point.

It also opens RER F, from the northern suburbs through Paris Nord-Est and Saint-Lazare to the west. At Paris Nord-Est it builds the 6 TGV and 6 RER F platforms; the 4 regional express and 4 RER G platforms follow in the second stage, beside them assumption. The regional express links in the Nord-Est throats and at the north and east ramps, most of the €0.65 billion of works for those links, are built in the first stage, so that the open station need not be disturbed later assumption. Gare de Lyon is built with all its 8 tracks; its two new ones take the sixteenth south-eastern TGV an hour from the first opening, and its regional express trains keep the surface until they can run through to Nord-Est in the second stage. Whether the Nord-Est platforms of the second stage can be dug later without disturbing the open ones, or should be dug with them, is a study point. The junction cavern for the link would be dug with Gare de Lyon, so that the link can be joined later without closing the station; its cost is counted in the second stage assumption.
  • What it leaves. Atlantic trains still end at Montparnasse: the first stage alone gives no through train to or from the Atlantic. A passenger from Bordeaux to Lille still crosses Paris by metro, and the direct link between the two southern stations does not exist. The regional express trains and lines P and N, the future RER G, still end on the surface at Gare du Nord, Gare de l’Est, Montparnasse, Gare de Lyon and Bercy, so the surface tracks of those stations cannot all be freed, and their parks wait for the second stage.
  • What is not known. The benefits of the first stage on its own have not been estimated. Whether the works should be staged at all, and whether the Atlantic could come first, has not been studied: staging is a study point.

Whether to stop after the first stage cannot be judged yet, because its benefits on their own have not been estimated; see building in stages. The whole cost is built up in the cost chapter.

Twelve years, year by year

An assumed schedule

The model assumes 12 years of works with even spending assumption. How those years divide between tasks and stages is an illustration made for this page. It is not a construction programme: there is no design, no ground investigation and no study of how many platforms each terminal can give up while it stays open.

Move through the years to see what is being built, what is open and what passengers find at each station.

Is twelve years plausible?

Smaller projects of the same kind took seven to thirteen years, and one is past twenty. Montparnasse (14 tracks), Gare de Lyon and Saint-Lazare (8 each) are smaller than Paris Nord-Est and may take less time. The second stage holds most of the tunnel, 25.3 km of 44.5: boring it in about five years would need several machines at once, as on the Elizabeth line, where eight machines bored 42 km in three years.73 Whether that shortens or lengthens the critical path of the second stage is to be checked.

A longer schedule costs money as well as time, because interest runs during the works. Over 12 years it adds 20% to the cost. If the works took 15 years, the yearly cost of the project would rise by 4.0%; see the sensitivity tests.

Assumed here

  • 12 years of works, with even spending.
  • The first stage opens after year 9, the second after year 12.
  • Every terminal stays open until its deep station is ready.
  • Each park opens some years after its surface tracks close, once the tracks are cleared: those of Gare du Nord, Gare de l’Est, Montparnasse, Gare de Lyon and Bercy after the second stage, when the last regional and suburban trains leave their surface platforms; part of the Gare de Lyon TGV tracks may be freed after the first.

Not known

  • The design of any station, and so the method and time needed to build it. The same for the link and its two junction caverns.
  • The ground, the groundwater and the old quarries at each site.
  • How many platforms each terminal can give up during the works.
  • Where the shafts and work sites would go, and how the spoil would leave. At Zürich, up to three trains of spoil left the site each day.67
  • How long studies, public inquiry and approvals would take before the first year.
Chapter 5

Which trains run where

The same pattern of trains is assumed every hour, and no train reverses in Paris. A high-speed train runs from the north or the east to one of the two southern stations through Paris Nord-Est, or between the two southern stations by the direct link, so each train stops at two of the three stations. In a standard busy hour, 12 trains each way run from the north or east to the south and 6 each way run between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon by the link. That pattern, with room kept for the day the southern lines are full, sets the number of platforms. Regional express trains run in the same tunnels, in the 2-minute paths between the TGVs.

One standard hour of high-speed trains

  • Every train stops twice in Paris, and never turns. A train from Bordeaux stops at Montparnasse, then either at Nord-Est, going on to Lille or Strasbourg, or at Gare de Lyon by the direct link, going on to Marseille. A train from Lille stops at Nord-Est, then at Gare de Lyon or at Montparnasse. Every station has direct trains to all four directions, on half of the trains of each line.
  • The same pattern every hour. The study assumes that the same trains run at the same minutes every hour, on one beat at all three stations: the timetable builds that hour, and the travel times and the platform count of this report use its figures.
  • Platforms are fixed. The 14:07 to Lyon leaves from the same platform every day, printed in the timetable, with the place of each coach marked on the platform.62 What that changes for boarding is in the three stations.
  • High-speed trains are not for trips inside Paris. Tickets are sold from or to a station outside the region.

How many trains is a standard hour? This study takes 12 TGVs an hour each way on the Atlantic line, 12 on the south-east line, 8 on the northern line and 4 on the eastern line assumption. These are round numbers for a busy hour, not counts; the real pattern has to come from a timetable study, and what caps the number of trains today, platforms or lines, is a study point (I1 in what to verify). The second pattern below fills the two southern lines to their planned capacity: 16 trains an hour on the line to Lyon from 2030,17 and up to 15 on the Atlantic line with new signalling.6 83 No capacity figure was found for the northern and eastern lines; they are held at 8 and 4 assumption.

Any line can be paired with any other

The tunnels join all four lines, so a train arriving from one line can leave by any of the others: the northern and eastern lines meet the two southern ones at Nord-Est, and the two southern lines meet each other by the link. The timetable is free to pair them as traffic requires, and to change the pairing from one hour to the next. The choice holds at every station: from each of the three, there are direct trains in all four directions.

The four lines are not equal. The two southern lines carry more than twice the passengers of the northern and eastern ones: about 44 and 35 million a year counted at their Paris terminals, against 21.5 and 12 (derived).84 So not every train from the south can find a partner in the north or the east. In the standard hour, 4 trains from each southern line go on to the north and 2 to the east, which uses every train of the northern and eastern lines. The 6 trains left on each southern line are paired with each other by the direct link, with no reversal. When the southern lines are full, 9 an hour each way take the link and 1 south-east train an hour is left without a partner: it runs on through Nord-Est to the east line, as a new hourly link. No train turns back anywhere.

For passengers, this gives direct trains on five of the six pairs of lines; only north to east has none, because the two lines meet just north of Nord-Est. Crossing Paris by TGV gives the times for each pair. Fixed pairs, with each southern line tied to one northern line, would be simpler to run but would leave only two pairs with direct trains; the model no longer tests that case, since the link makes it unnecessary.

A train from Bordeaux stops at Montparnasse, runs 5 km under the south of Paris to Gare de Lyon, stops there and continues to Marseille. The link gives direct trains between the Atlantic and the south-east, the largest flow across Paris, in 13 minutes instead of 34 by Nord-Est with a reversal, and it keeps Nord-Est for the trains that need it.

  • What it does to the load. With the lines full, the three legs carry 6, 7 and 9 trains an hour each way. Without the link the two legs to Nord-Est would carry 15 and 16, and every Atlantic to south-east train would have to change direction at Nord-Est.
  • Length and time are assumptions. The link is taken as 5 km, within 4.5 to 6 depending on the alignment, and the 13 minutes are a 6-minute run and the 7-minute stop assumption. Its geometry under the south of Paris, where old quarries lie,41 has not been designed: study point I7 in what to verify.
  • A new link to the east. With the south-east line at 16 trains an hour, 1 train an hour has no partner on any line. Instead of turning back, it stops at Gare de Lyon and Nord-Est and runs on to the east line, towards Reims or Strasbourg: a new hourly link, like the fourth eastern regional train. Nord-Est then sees 13 plain stops an hour each way, and the east approach 9 trains an hour with the regional ones, the least busy of the four (23% at 1.5-minute signalling). No train reverses in Paris.assumption

How many platforms

The rule. Platforms are dedicated by direction: the tracks on one side of a station take trains heading south, those on the other side trains heading north, as at any through station. A stop takes 7 minutes; the track is then held 2 minutes more for a late train, and after the departure it needs about 3 minutes before the next train can pull in. Each train therefore takes a place of 12 minutes, and one track takes 5 trains an hour assumption, all three figures, the beat of the timetable. Through stations elsewhere give the measure: Stuttgart's new station reached about six trains an hour on each track in a simulated stress test,8 9 Zürich's Löwenstrasse handles about 460 trains a day on four tracks, about six an hour on each on average,10 and Tokyo's Shinagawa was built with four tracks for 15 trains an hour each way.85 Through trains that wait for connections in Zürich stand 6 to 9 minutes (derived from the departure boards; see Zürich).11 12

Three tracks each way, and a fourth at Gare de Lyon. With the lines full, each station sees 13 to 16 stops an hour in each direction. Three tracks each way take 15, one place every 4 minutes on a side, and the margin for late trains is inside each place, the 2 minutes held after each departure. The Atlantic line's 15 trains an hour fit with nothing to spare; the 16 planned on the south-east line by 2030 would not fit on three, by one train an hour. Shorter stops would free places: with 5-minute stops a place would be 10 minutes and a track would take 6 trains an hour, but passengers with luggage need time to board and alight a 400 m train, and Lyon Part-Dieu plans 6 minutes for most TGVs. So Gare de Lyon has a fourth track each way, 8 in all: it takes the 16th train of the hour and the regional express trains to Burgundy (see below).

The sliders change the rule, not the timetable: a longer stop, a longer clearing time or a lower share of the hour used all mean fewer trains on each track.

Regional express trains: in the TGV tunnels, on platforms of their own

Regional express trains (TER) have no tunnel of their own: they run in the TGV tunnels. The paths through the tunnels are laid on a grid of 2 minutes, 30 an hour each way. The TGVs keep their places of the 12-minute beat, one every 4 minutes on each side, and the TER take the paths in between. Nothing changes for TGV passengers: the 2 minutes held after each stop become the window between the public departure, when the doors close at the time printed in the timetable, and the railway departure, when the train leaves in its path. Every train, TGV or TER, takes the same 6 minutes between two stations, so the paths never cross.

The condition is the signalling. Trains must be able to follow each other about 1.5 minutes apart in the tunnels: European train control at level 2 (ETCS, the signals shown in the driver's cab) with short sections, and automatic driving in the tunnels assumption. Planners keep the busiest hour under 75% of what a line can carry, the usual European guidance (UIC leaflet 406, unverified). At 1.5 minutes every tunnel stays under that line, the busiest at 65%; at 2 minutes the Atlantic approach would reach 87%.

Which TER run through. In the peak hour, each way, the 11 regional express trains of Gare du Nord run through Nord-Est to Montparnasse and on to the Atlantic lines, towards Chartres, Le Mans and Granville, so that side gets 11 an hour instead of the 7 of today. The 3 of Gare de l'Est, with 1 new regional train an hour, run through Nord-Est to Gare de Lyon and on to Burgundy, which has 4 today assumption. All the TER of Gare de Lyon and of Bercy thus go underground and run through to Nord-Est, so the Bercy station is freed. No TER turns back in Paris. Northern TER leave the TGV tracks at Nord-Est by plain turnouts; eastern ones cross the TGV lines by one dive-under at each end of the station. Joining the TER to the TGV tunnels, at the station throats and at three of the TGV portals, is carried at €0.65 billion before mark-ups assumption.

Platform time. A TER holds its platform 7 minutes, a stop of 5 with margin for late running and 2 before the next train can pull in; a TGV holds it 12 assumption. Nord-Est and Montparnasse each have 4 TER platform tracks, two each way, 350 m long; the length takes three coupled Regio 2N sets, which are 81 to 135 m each (unverified). At Gare de Lyon the TER stop on the fourth TGV track each way. How many TER an hour each line would run through Paris is study point I3 in what to verify.
