At Gare de Lyon the TER stop on the fourth high-speed track each way. The two new suburban lines, RER G (today’s lines P and N, joined) and RER F (today’s lines H, K and L), each have their own twin-track tunnel; the TER share the TGV tunnels. Between Nord-Est and Montparnasse two tunnels run side by side, the TGV tunnel, with the TER in it, and RER G. Between Nord-Est and Gare de Lyon, and on the direct link, there is only the TGV tunnel. The number of trains an hour a regional or suburban track takes is the plan's assumption.

Line R: a later option

Suburban line R stays on the surface at Gare de Lyon, on a small terminal of a few tracks; it is the one open item left there. It cannot simply use the two new tracks: the fourth track each way is already busy 40 of 60 minutes (67%) with the 16th TGV and the TER, and with the 5 trains an hour of line R it would need 70, more than one track can give. R would also have to run on through Nord-Est, where the TER tracks would go to 135 of 120 minutes. So R needs 2 tracks of its own at Gare de Lyon and 2 at Nord-Est, 330 m long, about €2.1 billion with all mark-ups assumption. The south-east tunnel itself could take it: 25 trains an hour, 63% of its capacity with trains 1.5 minutes apart, so no extra approach tunnel is needed for R. Its partner beyond Nord-Est would be extra trains on the branches of today's line P towards Meaux or Provins. With no proven demand for them, about €2.1 billion for 5 trains an hour is left as a later option, kept open for the growth that line R may see.

Suburban trains: RER G and RER F

  • RER G joins today’s lines P and N into one line, with its own twin-track tunnel, 11.5 km, from the eastern approach through Nord-Est to Montparnasse and out on the Atlantic side. Trains of line P from the east run on through Nord-Est and Montparnasse to the south-west, and the other way. It has 4 platform tracks of 225 m at Nord-Est and 4 at Montparnasse. A suburban track takes 10 trains an hour (the plan) assumption, so 20 each way, against a peak today of 11 an hour on line P and 12 on line N, 16 on line N with the Clamart plan (the plan).
  • RER F joins today’s lines H, K and L into one line: the branches of line L become further branches of RER F. Its new twin-track tunnel, 6.2 km, runs from the northern approach under Nord-Est to a new deep through station under Saint-Lazare, then back up onto the Batignolles and Pont-Cardinet tracks. The ride from Nord-Est to Saint-Lazare takes 4 minutes. It has 6 platform tracks of 225 m at Nord-Est and 6 at Saint-Lazare, so 30 trains an hour each way at 10 a track assumption, against a peak of 20 on line H and 3 on line K, 23 together, on the northern side and 24 to 28 on line L on the western side (the plan). Line J and the trains to Normandy stay in Saint-Lazare's surface station.
  • Unequal sides. On both lines one side runs a few more trains than the other at the peak: line N with the Clamart plan against line P, line L against lines H and K. Those trains have no partner across Paris; where they turn back is not yet studied. Whether 4 and 6 tracks are enough at the peak is study point I4 in what to verify.

London trains and depots

  • London trains board from one of the six high-speed tracks at Nord-Est, closed off for each departure, with a larger control hall and waiting room above it (counted at €200 million of works assumption). At about one departure an hour and 10 to 15 minutes of boarding, that fits within the rule above. Amsterdam already boards London trains this way, from one closed-off platform.28 Trains arriving from London are checked before departure, so they can run on to the south like any other. Northbound, passengers boarding at a southern station for London would need to be checked before boarding: how, and where, is open (study point I5). Today's cross-Channel terminal at Gare du Nord is itself at its limits.27
  • Depots stay where they are; trains reach them through the tunnel portals (see changes on the surface).

Regional express and suburban trains through Paris

Each of the new tunnels joins lines from both sides of Paris. Regional express trains from the north run through Nord-Est to Montparnasse and on to the lines towards Chartres, Le Mans and Granville; those from the east run through Nord-Est to Gare de Lyon and on to Burgundy, and the other way. Line P from the east runs on along line N towards Versailles and Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines, as RER G; lines H and K from the north run on through Saint-Lazare onto the branches of line L, as RER F. Line R does not run through. So three pairs of suburban lines have direct trains across Paris, H with L, K with L and P with N, and three more have one easy change at Nord-Est, between lines H or K and line N, and between line P and line L.

The point is less the second station than what lies beyond it. RER G joins the residential north-east and east to the research, university and company clusters of the south-west, around Versailles, Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines and the Saclay plateau. RER F gives the northern suburbs a ride without a change to Clichy-Levallois, Pont-Cardinet, Courbevoie and La Défense, relieving RER line E, full in the morning, and joins Saint-Lazare and the western suburbs directly to Gare du Nord and its trains to the airport. Few people cross Paris from suburb to suburb today because it is so hard, not for lack of reasons to: the Grand Paris Express line 15 was built on that idea. What the through trains are worth to their passengers is in regional and suburban passengers, and the job access they open in the economic return.

Chapter 6

How long to reach a station where your train stops

From the average point in Paris, a station where your TGV, the French high-speed train, stops is 27.4 minutes away today by public transport. With the three through stations it is 22.8 minutes to the entrance of the nearest station where the train stops, the measure used for the benefits of TGV passengers, or 23.2 minutes if the train’s 6-minute run between its Paris stops is counted and the passenger picks a train that calls at their best station. The stations stay where they are and the project only adds places to board, so no point in Paris is further from its train than today, for any direction.

The map: 1,000 points in Paris

Each dot is a point in Paris. Its colour shows the time by public transport from the street to a station where a TGV for the chosen direction stops. Choose a view, a way of counting and a direction, then tap a dot to read its times.

Legend

    All 1,000 points

    One point

    Tap or hover a dot to see, for each direction, where you board today and where you would board with the project.

    What “with the project” counts

    Today each direction has one terminal: Gare du Nord for the north, Gare de l’Est for the east, Gare de Lyon for the south-east, Montparnasse for the Atlantic. With the project every high-speed train stops at two of the three stations in Paris, no train changes direction, and a passenger boards at whichever stop suits best. Today’s station is always one of them. That is why the time can only get shorter.

    Trains forEvery train stops atHalf of the trains also stop at
    The north and the eastParis Nord-Est, entered from the Gare du Nord hall or from the Gare de l’Est hallGare de Lyon, for the half that come up from the south-east; Montparnasse, for the half that come up from the Atlantic
    The south-eastGare de LyonParis Nord-Est, for the half that come down from the north or the east; Montparnasse, for the half that come from the Atlantic by the direct link between the two southern stations, a run of 6 minutes
    The AtlanticMontparnasseParis Nord-Est, for the half that come down from the north or the east; Gare de Lyon, for the half that come from the south-east by the direct link, a run of 6 minutes

    Which trains run where is set out in how the lines are paired and the direct link. The even split between the two other stations is an assumption, and so is free entry to Paris Nord-Est from both halls. The second one matters: with entry from the Gare du Nord side only, the Paris average at the station entrance would be 23.1 minutes and not 22.8, and people who live nearer to Gare de l’Est would be further from a train for the east than today.

    There are two honest ways to count the result. The map offers both.

    To the station entrance

    22.8 minutes on average, 4.6 fewer than today.

    The minutes by public transport from a point in Paris to the entrance of the nearest station where the train stops. Where only half of the trains stop at the nearest station, the map takes the average of the two halves.

    This answers the plain question: how far am I from a station where my train stops? It is the measure used for the benefits of TGV passengers. On a trip of two or three hours, the few minutes the train then spends under Paris are spent seated on the right train with nothing more to carry or find; what matters to these passengers is a short trip to the station and no change on the way assumption. On this count 100% of the points are quicker than today, by up to 9.4 minutes.

    Counting the ride across Paris

    23.2 minutes on average, 4.1 fewer than today.

    The same, plus the train’s ride between its Paris stops when you board at the first one: the 6-minute run between any two of the three stations, by the link between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon as through Nord-Est. The 7-minute stop is not counted against the passenger, because the train is already at the platform when they reach it; the TGV measure of crossing Paris, for someone who stays on board, still counts it (13 minutes). The passenger picks, among the trains for their direction, one that calls at the station that suits them best, as someone who cares about time would soon learn to do, and boards at the first stop only when that still puts them ahead. It assumes enough trains an hour to choose from without a longer wait assumption, which holds on the busy lines and less so on the east.

    This answers a stricter question: how much sooner am I on my way? It is shown for TGV passengers as a test, and it is the way regional and suburban passengers are counted, for whom a few minutes matter on a short trip. On this count 99% of the points are quicker, by up to 11.6 minutes, and the rest are unchanged.

    An example. Point 275 on the map is in the 15th arrondissement, a few hundred metres from Montparnasse. Someone who lives there and travels to Lyon crosses Paris by metro to Gare de Lyon today: 29.1 minutes. With the project half of the Lyon trains come from the Atlantic, stop at Montparnasse, 4.6 minutes away, and run through the link to Gare de Lyon in 6 minutes. The other half come down from Nord-Est, and for those Gare de Lyon stays the place to board. The first measure averages the two halves at the door: 15.7 minutes. The second has the passenger always take a link train and adds the 6-minute run on the link, because until Gare de Lyon this passenger is no nearer to Lyon than someone who boards there: 10.6 minutes. The minutes on the link are spent in a seat on the right train and not in the metro, which is worth something, but they are still minutes.

    Which measure the model uses

    The time saved by TGV passengers from the Paris region, and the extra TGV journeys it brings, come from the first measure, to the station entrance. The second measure is kept as a test in the sensitivity tests. Regional express and suburban passengers are counted the other way: their gain counts the train’s ride to the station that suits them, and assumes they pick a train that goes there, in regional trains.

    The map does not include the time inside the station, from the entrance to the coach, which is a separate matter treated in boarding in a deep station; the model also tests what happens if every passenger needs two more minutes than today, in the sensitivity tests.

    How the 1,000 times were computed. A grid of 1,000 points, 315 m apart, covers Paris without its two woods. From each point the model finds the shortest time to the hall of each station on foot, by metro, RER and tram, with the average wait for each line, on the network of Île-de-France Mobilités as of 5 October 2026.86 Buses, taxis and crowding are not counted. The four directions are weighted by their share of high-speed traffic: Atlantic 39%, south-east 31%, north 19%, east 11% (derived).84 The full method is in how access times are computed.

    Who gains, and what it is worth

    Every direction gains. At the station entrance the north and the Atlantic gain most (4.8 and 4.8 minutes), the south-east least (4.2): every train also stops at a second station, Nord-Est on the other side of the city or the other southern station through the link. Once the ride is counted, a train for Lille boarded at Gare de Lyon or Montparnasse reaches Nord-Est in a 6-minute run, and a train for Lyon boarded at Montparnasse reaches Gare de Lyon in the same 6. On that count the four directions come out close together: 23.5 minutes for the south-east, 23.1 for the Atlantic and 23.3 for the north and the east, because the run from the first station takes back part of what the second place to board saves.

    Minutes, Paris averageTrafficTodayAt the entranceSavedCounting the rideSaved
    North (Lille, London, Brussels)19%27.622.84.823.34.4
    East (Reims, Strasbourg)11%27.222.84.423.33.9
    South-east (Lyon, Marseille)31%27.623.44.223.54.1
    Atlantic (Bordeaux, Rennes, Nantes)39%27.122.34.823.14.1
    All directions, weighted by traffic100%27.422.84.623.24.1

    Even with the ride counted, the first stop is the better choice for a good part of Paris: for 52% of the points a train for the south-east is better boarded where it stops first, at Nord-Est or at Montparnasse, than at Gare de Lyon, and for 48% a train for the Atlantic is better boarded at Nord-Est or at Gare de Lyon than at Montparnasse. For trains to the north, 19% of the points do better at Gare de Lyon and 34% at Montparnasse, on the trains that stop there.

    The north-east of Paris gains most at the door. The 19th and 10th arrondissements (the districts of Paris) lie around and beyond Nord-Est, where every train for the north and the east, and half of the others, would stop. Today their residents cross the city for a train to Lyon or Bordeaux. Their station entrance comes 7.1 and 7.1 minutes closer on average, or 7.9 and 8.0 minutes with the ride counted. Once the ride is counted, the south-west joins them. The 15th and 14th, around Montparnasse, save 6.9 and 5.7 minutes, close to the north-east: the link puts a train for the south-east a 6-minute run from Montparnasse, where today it is a metro ride across the city. The smallest gains are in the west and the centre: in the 8th, the 17th and the 5th the entrance comes 1.8, 1.9 and 2.1 minutes closer, and less once the ride is counted (0.4, 0.4 and 0.8 minutes). These districts are about as far from one station as from another, so a second place to board helps them little.

    The numbers by arrondissement

    The suburbs gain a little more than Paris, because their trains and RER lines arrive on one side of the city. At the station entrance the model finds 4.6 minutes saved for a trip that starts in Paris, 5.0 in the inner suburbs and 6.5 in the outer suburbs. The map shows Paris only.

    What quicker access is worth in the model

    The model counts the whole Paris region, at the station entrance, in “equivalent minutes”: the official French method counts a minute of walking or changing as two and a minute of waiting as one and a half, because passengers dislike them more than sitting in a train.87 On that scale the average trip to the train is 5.9 minutes shorter.

    That is worth €354 million a year in time saved and brings about 2.83 million more high-speed journeys a year: British ticket data give about 11% more traffic for 10% less journey time.88 If the train’s 6-minute run between its Paris stops were counted against the passenger, who then picks a train that calls at their best station, the trip would be 5.7 equivalent minutes shorter, worth €344 million a year and 2.75 million journeys; the model keeps that as a test, not as the central case.

    Almost all of it comes from the choice of station. With the same three stations but each train boarded only at its own, the gain would be €27 million a year. The choice between two places to board is worth €326 million a year.

    These journeys are part of the high-speed traffic forecast, and the time saved is one line of the benefits.

    Chapter 7

    The timetable: an evenly spaced hour at the three stations

    All three stations work to the same clock. Each train takes a place of 12 minutes on its track, the platform rule of the report (see how many platforms), and every run between two stations is made to take 6 minutes, so trains from outside Paris arrive at every station at :00, :04, :08 and every 4 minutes after. Three tracks each way take 15 trains an hour: the southern lines full, with no place to spare. Today's busy hour fits with 3 places free on each side.

    A sketch of a timetable, not a timetable

    The minutes below follow a few stated rules: the time a train stops and holds its track, the time a track stays empty between two trains, and the spacing of trains in a tunnel. No signalling, junction or driver has been studied. The whole report uses this beat: 7-minute stops and runs of 6 minutes between stations, as built here. The benefits count the travel times it gives, nothing for its regularity. The model is model/table_timetable.py, which runs in seconds.

    How the hour is built: one beat of 12 minutes

    7minstop at the platform, for every trainLyon Part-Dieu plans 6 for most TGVs (see why 7 minutes) assumption
    +2minthe track stays reserved after the planned departureRoom for a slightly late train assumption
    3minempty track before the next trainAs in the platform rule of the report assumption
    6minrun between any two of the stations5 minutes of running and 1 of margin; a design target assumption
    1. One place every 4 minutes. A train holds a track 12 minutes, so a track takes a train at :00, :12, :24, :36 and :48. Three tracks, each starting 4 minutes after the previous one, give one place every 4 minutes on a side of a station: 15 an hour, more than the 3 minutes two trains need between them in a tunnel.
    2. The same minutes everywhere. Trains from outside Paris arrive at all three stations at the same minutes. As every run takes 6 minutes, a train reaches its second station 13 minutes after its first, again on a place of the same beat, on the other side of that station.
    3. Each place sends three trains round the triangle. In each place each station sends its train to one of the two others, and no two trains go to the same station. So the three trains turn one way round the triangle (Montparnasse to Nord-Est, Nord-Est to Gare de Lyon, Gare de Lyon to Montparnasse) or the other way; when Nord-Est has no train in that place, Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon swap theirs by the link. The service plan sets how many places of each kind: with the southern lines full, 6 one way, 6 the other and 3 swaps, spread over the hour.
    HourMontparnasseGare de LyonParis Nord-Est
    Trains in and outFree placesTrains in and outFree placesTrains in and outFree places
    About today12 and 12612 and 12612 and 126
    Southern lines full15 and 15015 and 15012 and 126
    Nord-Est filled too15 and 15015 and 15015 and 150

    Three high-speed tracks on each side of each station, 15 places an hour on each. "In": trains from the station's own line; "out": trains going out to it. Every rule is checked on the finished hour (model).

    Room for delays. Today's busy hour leaves 3 free places an hour on every side, room for a late train or a train sent to another track. With the southern lines full, Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon have none: a late train would wait for the next free place or push the train behind it. One more track on each side of each station, kept for late trains, would be needed then. Gare de Lyon has one: its fourth high-speed track each way, not drawn here, takes the sixteenth south-east train of the hour and the regional express trains (TER), busy 40 of 60 minutes (see how many platforms). At Nord-Est and Montparnasse the TER have platforms of their own, so a track kept for late TGVs would be a seventh and eighth high-speed track; how many such tracks, and at which stations, is to be studied (study point I2 in what to verify).

    A standard beat. With the same minutes at every station and every track, staff and passengers learn one pattern; a late train takes the next place of the beat, a platform change moves a train to a track whose places are known, and the same recovery rules apply everywhere, as in Switzerland's regular timetable (see the Swiss pulse).

    The run of 6 minutes. The longest tunnel, Nord-Est to Montparnasse, is 6.0 km in the model. A train that starts at 0.4 m/s², runs at 100 km/h and brakes at 0.5 m/s² covers it in 5.0 minutes with a 7% margin, and the two other tunnels in 4.3 minutes assumption: 6 minutes leaves a minute of margin on every leg.

    With a 3-minute reserve instead of 2: four tracks each way when the southern lines are full

    With 3 minutes of reserve, a place takes 13 minutes and a track only 4 trains an hour. Filling track 1, then track 2, and so on, and letting trains leave up to the end of their reserve to fit the next station, gives:

Whether the lines, rather than the terminals, cap today's traffic is study point I1 in what to verify. The map and the clocks below show all three hours.

    The hour at the platforms and on the map, in step

    Press play: the three clocks and the map run the same hour together. Choose today's traffic or the most the three stations can take. Each train has the colour of the two lines it joins: darker towards the north or east, and from the Atlantic to the south-east; lighter the other way. The second tab, all trains, adds the others: TGVs become squares, regional express trains are ringed grey dots running in the TGV tunnels between the TGVs, and the two new suburban lines, RER G (today's lines P and N, joined) and RER F (today's lines H, K and L), are dots, one colour for each line, in their own tunnels.

    London trains, running through

    Today London trains end at Gare du Nord: 12 non-stop trains a day each way, from tracks closed off for the border checks. A passenger from Lyon to London crosses Paris between two stations and changes twice, at Paris and at London, a trip sold by Eurostar in about 5 h 30 (read on the operator's site, October 2026, unverified).

    In this timetable London trains are shown in their own colour, one an hour each way, running through Paris on a south-east path: from Marseille or Lyon they stop at Gare de Lyon and at Nord-Est, where the track they use is closed off for the border checks while their passengers, checked in the control hall, board assumption. Trains from London stop like any other: their passengers were checked before leaving London. Running through, a passenger from Lyon or Marseille stays on the same train to London. Passengers boarding in the south would be checked in a terminal of their own at Lyon or Marseille; whether that is done, and the same for Bordeaux by Montparnasse, is study point I5 in what to verify.

    Waits, direct trains and the one change

    2.0minaverage wait for a train to the Atlantic line2.0 to the south-east, 4.4 to the north, 7.6 to the east, from a random minute, with the southern lines full
    20minin Paris on a direct trainFrom the first Paris arrival to the last Paris departure: two stops of 7 minutes and one run of 6
    12minfrom a train from the north to one to the east, or backChange at Nord-Est included, on average

    With trains to every part of France calling at two of the three stations, a passenger crossing Paris finds a direct train for every pair of lines but one. About 50% of them are taken to find one for their own trip, as in the rest of the report; the others change once. Only between the north and the east is a change always needed, at Nord-Est.

    Against a pulse timed for changes. This study also searched for timetables with 4-minute stops, either spread evenly or timed so that each train meets as many others as possible, as a Swiss pulse would. Timing for changes shortened a change between two services by about 3 minutes against an untimed hour, but made the hour less regular, and few passengers change. The track-by-track hour above keeps trains as regular as their tracks allow.

    Why 7 minutes

    At a Paris stop roughly half of a full high-speed train gets off or on, with luggage, through few doors: a double-deck TGV has far fewer doors for each passenger than a suburban train. The stops planned today at the busiest through stations give the measure (own count from the timetable data):

    StationPlanned stop of most trains
    Lyon Part-Dieu, TGV6 minutes; 10 when two trains are coupled or split94
    Paris-Charles de Gaulle 2, Bordeaux, Rennes, TGV6 minutes94
    Smaller TGV stations3 minutes94
    Hamburg Hbf and Berlin Hbf, ICE4 minutes95
    Frankfurt and Stuttgart Hbf, ICE, where trains reverse6 minutes95
    Zürich, long-distance trains that wait for connections6 to 9 minutes (see Zürich)

    A Paris stop is closer to Lyon Part-Dieu than to Hamburg, so this study takes 7 minutes, with 2 minutes of reserve on the track assumption. Longer stops have a price. For every passenger crossing Paris there are about 7 who start or end their trip in Paris,84 and about half of them stay on board through one of the two stops, because their station is the train's second (derived from the 1,000 points of the access map). The chart, from an earlier search, counts what each length of stop adds against 4 minutes.

    What the timetable rests on

    • Spacing in the tunnels. 3 minutes between two trains on one track is about what the south-east line needs to carry the 16 trains an hour planned for it,17 and more than the 2.5 minutes of the Elizabeth line's central tunnel at 24 trains an hour.96 The beat of 4 minutes keeps the TGVs further apart than that; the TER between them bring the spacing down to 2 minutes (1.5 at 7 places in the hour with Nord-Est filled too), which is why the tunnels need signalling for about 1.5 (see below).
    • Regional express trains (TER) run in the TGV tunnels, on an hour of their own fitted between the TGVs by the model (model/ter_timetable.py, a constraint solver; model/table_timetable.py checks its result again against the TGV hour). They take the times between the TGV places, in half-minutes: on every track a TER shares, the train ahead and the train behind are at least 2 minutes away with the southern lines full (2 about today; with Nord-Est filled too, 1.5 at 7 places in the hour), which needs signalling for trains about 1.5 minutes apart assumption. A TER stops 5 minutes and its platform track then stays empty 2; where it has to wait for its path it stands longer: 31 of the hour's 60 TER stops, up to 8 minutes. The TER stop at platforms of their own at Nord-Est and Montparnasse and on the fourth high-speed track each way at Gare de Lyon. RER G (today's lines P and N) has its own tunnel from Nord-Est to Montparnasse, and RER F (today's lines H, K and L) its own from Nord-Est to Saint-Lazare. These trains, described in how many platforms, take no place from the high-speed trains. How many TER each line would run through Paris is study point I3 in what to verify. Suburban line R stays on the surface at Gare de Lyon.
    • Trains on time. A late train delays the train behind it on a full line, and the change between the north and the east. Regular timetables rest on punctual trains: in Switzerland more than nine in ten arrive within three minutes;97 see the Swiss timetable applied to Paris.
    • Destinations. The timetable fixes paths, not destinations: whether a path runs to Bordeaux or to Nantes, and how often each city is served, is a choice of service. The waits above are for the next train to a line, or between two lines.
    • Junctions. Trains crossing each other at the junctions north and south of Nord-Est and at the ends of the link are taken to do so on separate levels; the cost counts 4 junctions (see the prices used).
    Chapter 8

    Crossing Paris, by TGV and by regional train

    A passenger who crosses Paris today spends about an hour between two trains, with a metro ride in the middle. With the stations joined, five of the six pairs of lines get direct trains and none of them reverses: 20 minutes in Paris on a direct train for every pair, a 7-minute stop at each of its two stations and a 6-minute run between them, by the direct link from Montparnasse to Gare de Lyon or through Nord-Est for the others, and a change of train happens on the platforms of one station. Suburban and regional passengers gain less on each trip, 2.1 minutes on the clock on average, but there are 155 million such journeys a year.

    TGV passengers who cross Paris

    About 107 million journeys a year by TGV, the French high-speed train, touch Paris: 102 million start or end there and 5.2 million cross it, changing between two Paris stations, usually by metro or by RER, the express suburban lines that cross Paris underground. Those who cross are counted at two stations, which is why the four terminals count 112.5 million passengers. The 5.2 million is derived from the last survey, in 2012-13: 13,000 a day in the region, 88% of them in the stations inside Paris, all kinds of train together, scaled by the growth of high-speed traffic since.4 No newer count is published, and none by pair of stations. The shares below assume that pairs follow the traffic of each station assumption. A fresh count, from the operators' ticket data, is study point I12 in what to verify.

A direct train does not suit every trip, so the estimate assumes that 50% of the passengers on those pairs find one for their own journey assumption. That makes 47% of all passengers who cross Paris; the others change inside one station, Nord-Est for most pairs.
    • North to east has no direct train. The two lines meet just north of the station, and the plan sends every train of these two lines on to the south. This is the smallest of the six flows. Passengers change on the platforms instead of walking between two stations.
    • What it is worth. €512 million a year in time saved, counted the official way, which weighs a minute spent changing as two minutes on a train.87 If every passenger on a served pair found a direct train the project would add 12.2 million journeys a year across Paris; if none did, 8.4 million. The central estimate is 10.3 million: see how many more passengers.
    • What is not known. The number of passengers itself. Counting all 13,000 of the survey, on more days of the year, gives 7.3 million instead of 5.2 million. Ticket data held by the operators would settle it (study point I12).
    • London, Brussels, Amsterdam and Cologne. Trains from London are checked before departure, so they can run on to the south like any other, and so can the trains from Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany. Northbound, a passenger boarding at Gare de Lyon for London would need a check before boarding; how that is done is open (study point I5, see how many platforms).

    The market the count misses

    The survey counts people who already cross Paris by train. It does not count those who go by car or by air between the regions because of the change of station, nor those who take the trains that go round Paris on the bypass line, with stops at Marne-la-Vallée, Roissy and Massy: 21.9 million passengers in 2009, 17.6 million of them on trains through those outer stations.18 The example below shows why many of them would rather go through: for the pairs that include the Atlantic line, the trains round Paris are slow and few. Measuring that wider market is study point I13.

    Regional and suburban passengers

    Today the suburban lines H and K (Gare du Nord), P (Gare de l’Est), N (Montparnasse), L (Saint-Lazare) and R (Gare de Lyon) and the regional express trains end at their terminals, unlike the RER. In the plan each suburban line that runs through has its own tunnel and the regional express trains share the TGV tunnels, so each train stops at a second station, and passengers stay on board when that station is nearer to where they are going. Suburban passengers pay nothing more for it: the Navigo pass and the Île-de-France ticket already cover the metro ride they no longer make.

    The suburban lines become two through lines of the RER, F and G. RER F joins today’s lines H, K and L: the trains of lines H and K run under Nord-Est to a new deep through station under Saint-Lazare, 4 minutes on, stop included (the plan), and come back up on the tracks of line L, whose branches become further branches of RER F. Line L carries 297,000 trips a weekday; 88% of its trains would run through the tunnel, the others ending at the surface station, which stays for line J and the Normandy trains, and 50% of its riders start or end their trip at Saint-Lazare assumption. RER G joins today’s lines P and N: line P’s trains run through Nord-Est to Montparnasse and on along line N, and line N’s trains run on to Nord-Est. Line R stays on the surface at Gare de Lyon with no through running; its passengers see no change. Running it through to an eastern line is left as a later option.

    The point of these lines is not the second terminal: P’s riders already have ways to reach Montparnasse, and RER E already serves Saint-Lazare. It is what lies beyond. Today’s line N serves the south-west’s clusters of research, universities and companies, Versailles and Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines, towards Massy-Palaiseau, Polytechnique and Saclay; joined to line P as RER G, it puts the homes of the north-east and the east much closer to those highly qualified jobs, an employment corridor. RER F gives the northern suburbs a ride without a change to Clichy-Levallois, Pont-Cardinet, Courbevoie and La Défense, large job centres, and relieves RER E, full in the morning. It also joins Saint-Lazare and the western suburbs directly to Gare du Nord, for the airport: line K, and an easy change to RER B towards Roissy, Villepinte and Tremblay-en-France.

    47.3 million suburban passengers a year would use the second station (derived from the access model: 72% of the passengers of today’s line H, 51% of line P, 32% of line N and 29% of line L, none on line R). The minutes to Saint-Lazare are derived, not measured: the network data used for the other terminals do not include its new platforms, so for each point the model fits a straight line of minutes against distance on its times to Gare du Nord, Gare de l’Est and Montparnasse, reads it at the distance to Saint-Lazare, and takes the walk when that is shorter assumption.

    Regional express trains run through too, in the TGV tunnels, in the paths left between the TGVs (how the trains are paired). No regional express train turns back in Paris. The 11 trains an hour each way from the north run through Nord-Est to Montparnasse and on towards Chartres, Le Mans and Granville, so the Atlantic side goes from 7 to 11 trains an hour; the Atlantic trains run through to Nord-Est. The 3 from the east, with 1 new regional link an hour, run through Nord-Est to Gare de Lyon and on to Burgundy, and all of Gare de Lyon’s regional express trains, Bercy’s included, go underground and run through to Nord-Est, which frees the Bercy regional station. 22.1 million regional express passengers a year would get off at the second station: 72% of those from the north at Montparnasse, 43% of those from the east at Gare de Lyon, 32% of the Atlantic passengers and 17% of the south-eastern ones at Nord-Est. 2.8 million would cross Paris without leaving the train, taken as 5% of today’s passengers on the lines that run through plus the gain from the change removed assumption; a count of them is study point I15.

    Trains are assumed to take 7 minutes between Nord-Est and Montparnasse, the same 6-minute run as the TGV and a stop of 1 minute assumption. The saving for each passenger is the difference between the trip from the old terminal to their destination in Paris and the trip from whichever of the two stops is nearer, measured on the public transport network as in reaching the station. It counts only the minutes gained to reach places in Paris near the second station. The employment corridors, the jobs and campuses beyond the stations, are counted apart in the economic return, on the census commuting flows and the region's timetable.

    The numbers as a table

    Million journeys a year. The total saves 2.1 minutes on average.

    155 million journeys a year save 2.1 minutes on the clock on average, and more with the official weights on walking and waiting, which is how the value of €154 million a year is counted.87 For today’s line H, about 42% of the saving comes from being able to enter Nord-Est by either of its two halls, the rest from the second stop.

    Why two minutes matter

    • Fewer people change onto the metro and the RER at the terminals. Gare du Nord and Gare de l’Est together see 800,000 travellers a day.5 A commuter from the northern suburbs who works near Saint-Lazare or in La Défense no longer goes down to RER E at Magenta: the train goes there.
    • Crowding counts. In a survey of Île-de-France passengers, a minute in a full metro weighed up to 1.39 times a minute in an uncrowded one when seated, and 1.55 when standing.99 The estimate carries the comfort gained at €46 million a year, in the proportion found in the appraisal of the Grand Paris Express.100 The relief of each metro line is not modelled.
    • Counted elsewhere: the employment corridors beyond the stations and the relief of the crowded metro and RER legs are valued in the economic return, on the census commuting flows and the region's timetable; more frequent trains if the lines are rebuilt as through lines are not. Trips from one suburb to another across Paris are estimated below; the region’s travel model would confirm them: study point I14. The traffic these lines could gain is in how many more passengers.

    From one suburb to another, without the metro

    A passenger from Sarcelles who works in Courbevoie changes twice today: off line H at Gare du Nord, onto RER E to Saint-Lazare, and onto line L. With the plan the same passenger stays on the same train, now RER F. A passenger from Meaux bound for Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines also changes twice today, at Gare de l’Est and at Montparnasse, and with the plan stays on RER G. A passenger from Sarcelles bound for Versailles changes once, on the platforms of Nord-Est, from one suburban train to another.

    Such trips are rare today because they are nearly impossible, not for lack of demand. That is the reasoning behind line 15 of the Grand Paris Express, a ring from suburb to suburb. Each change costs passengers. British ticket data show that a journey with one more change of train loses 37% of its passengers;88 a trip that needs two changes keeps 40% of those it would have with none. The estimate removes both changes for the pairs of lines joined by a direct train, and one and a half for the others, a change across one platform counting as half a change assumption.

    How many such trips are made today is not counted by line. The 2012-13 station survey found that 14% of the trips through the Paris stations, 145,000 a weekday, run between two suburban départements and only pass through Paris.4 The estimate takes 20% of them, on lines H, K and P on one side and N, L and R on the other, as bound for a suburban line on the other side of Paris, and shares them between the nine pairs of lines in proportion to the residents along one line and the jobs along the other, fewer as the trip gets longer assumption. Line L’s corridor is taken as about 900 thousand residents and 450 thousand jobs, 25 minutes from Paris assumption.

    Chapter 9

    What it would cost to build

    No design exists yet, so the cost is built from quantities (kilometres of tunnel, metres of platform) and from what stations and tunnels have cost once built. The project comes to about €42 billion, between €28 billion and €62 billion with low and high prices. The four deep stations are the largest item; the tunnels, one for each kind of train, come next. The regional express trains have no tunnel of their own: they run in the TGV tunnels, which costs only the links that lead them in.

Gare de Lyon has 8 tracks of 400 m: the two added, one each way, carry the sixteenth south-east TGV of the hour and the 4 regional express trains an hour each way that run through to Nord-Est, so it needs no regional express tracks of its own. Saint-Lazare is a deep through station for RER F only; it needs no hall conversion, since its surface station stays for line J and the Normandy trains. The 5 km is an estimate from the map, 4.5 to 6 km assumption.

    Regional express trains in the TGV tunnels

    The regional express trains (TER) share the TGV tunnels instead of having a tunnel of their own. Paths in the tunnels are two minutes apart, 30 an hour each way; the TGVs keep their places in the 12-minute beat and the regional express trains take the paths in between (see the service). This needs signalling for trains about 1.5 minutes apart assumption. What must still be built is the way in: the regional express tracks have to reach the TGV tracks at both ends of the two stations where they have platforms of their own, Nord-Est and Montparnasse, and the existing regional lines have to reach the tunnels at their portals. The item is €0.65 billion before the add-ons, €0.95 billion all-in (derived) assumption:

    • six tie-ins in the station throats, where the regional express tracks join the TGV tracks (four at Nord-Est, two at Montparnasse), €0.05 billion each;
    • two dive-unders in the throats of Nord-Est, where the eastern and Gare de Lyon regional trains pass under the TGV lines, €0.10 billion each;
    • links at three TGV portals (north, east, Atlantic), where the regional lines join the tunnel ramps, €0.05 billion each.

    No project publishes a price for such links; the figures are assumptions, set below the price of a portal or a junction because each is a smaller work. The tunnels, junctions and portals are those of the TGV, so the regional express trains add no kilometre of tunnel.

    Open item: line R. Line R stays on the surface at Gare de Lyon, on a small terminal. Running it through to an eastern line would need two more tracks at Gare de Lyon and two at Nord-Est, about €2.1 billion all-in (derived), for 5 trains an hour with no proven partner; it is left as a later option and not costed in the total. Cross-check: the same unit prices gave €40.5 billion for the earlier triangle and €44.1 billion for the plan with a separate regional express tunnel; running the regional express trains in the TGV tunnels instead brings the total to €41.7 billion, 2.4 billion less (derived).

    Why 15%

    The usual allowance for a study estimate is about 30%, and that is what this estimate carried at first. It is now 15%, for three reasons.

    • The unit prices are final costs or signed contracts, not early estimates. The first RER E figure is the final cost of the line, which includes its 44% overrun.64 The RER E stations of 2024 are the contracts of 2016 to 2018.21 70 Zürich is a final cost;101 London is the cost of the station contracts as forecast near the end of the works.102 The Grand Paris figures are contracts and the files revised in 2017.100 103 104 A price that already holds an overrun needs a smaller margin than a price taken from a study.
    • The earlier figure counted some things twice. The station price was first grossed up by 1.27, then by 1.30, for design, land and risk, before 30% was added again on everything. For the stations that counted design and land partly twice. The price is now the all-in figure from Paris, and the add-ons are applied once.
    • The back-test says where the prices sit. Before risk, they come out 28% above the first RER E section and 39% above Zürich, but 20% to 34% below the RER E extension and far below Munich (see does the method hold).

    What the 15% still covers: stations deeper than any built in Paris, under terminals that stay open throughout; and the items for which no project publishes a price (junction caverns, portals, the conversion of the halls), 14% of the works. Two study points remain: a check, item by item, of which published prices are all-in (I9), and a risk allowance set item by item instead of one rate on everything (I10).

    The prices used, and where they come from

    1. Quantities come from the layout: 45 km of two-track tunnel and 15,300 m of platform track. Platforms are 400 m for TGVs, 350 m for regional express trains and 225 m for suburban trains. The regional express length holds three coupled Regio 2N sets, which are 81 to 135 m long each (unverified).23
    2. Unit prices come from built projects, brought to 2026 euros with the French public-works index.105 That index follows contractors' costs. Prices for underground work around Paris have risen faster: the Grand Paris Express by about 15 points more between 2012 and 2020 (derived).104 Older projects are therefore understated.
    3. Design and client costs add 20%, the SNCF convention at this stage (12% and 8%).106 Land bought adds 7%; 5% to 10% is usual.107
    4. Risk adds 15% on top, for the reasons given above. The Grand Paris Express carries 24% to 32% since 2017 on prices that were estimates.104 The RER E extension carried 6% and ended 45% over budget.72

    Why €1.0 million per metre. The evidence from Paris points two ways. The first RER E stations, Saint-Lazare and Magenta, have four tracks each in caverns 30 m down, like the ones needed here. The whole 1999 line cost €2.5 billion in today's money, final; with its 4 km of tunnel deducted at our price, the stations come to about €0.9 million per metre, everything included (derived).64 The two-track stations opened in 2024 cost €0.9 million to €1.4 million per metre for their structure alone, before fit-out.21 70 The price used sits between them: it leans high against the one complete Paris figure and low against London. With design, client costs, land and risk, a metre of platform track is carried at €1.46 million, so one 400 m TGV track at about €0.58 billion all-in.

    Not priced separately: the caverns at each end of a station where two tracks fan out into many. They are taken as covered by the station price, as in a French study of a four-track deep station whose box is 938 m long for 365 m of platform.54 For a station of 20 tracks this is untested.

    Try other prices

    Move the prices within what built projects show, and the risk with them. The total and the yearly repayment follow. The repayment is what the capital account has to find each year.

    Result

    The number of TGV tracks per station can be moved too. Four-track TGV stations were ruled out as too tight for the timetable (see how many platforms); the slider shows what they would save, not that they would work. It changes the TGV tracks at Nord-Est and Montparnasse, and at Gare de Lyon by the same number, which keeps its two extra tracks for the regional express trains and the sixteenth south-east TGV; Saint-Lazare has none.

    Does the method hold?

    The same prices were applied to seven projects that have been built or priced, and compared with their published cost.

    • Paris, first RER E section, built. The prices overshoot: €3.2 billion before risk, €3.7 billion with it, against a final cost of €2.5 billion that already includes a 44% overrun. The index used to bring 2003 money to 2026 is a floor, so the gap is smaller than it looks.
    • Paris, RER E extension, built. The prices undershoot: €4.6 billion before risk against €5.8 to €7.1 billion, depending on the price base of the published figure. With 15% risk, €5.3 billion, still 8% below the low reading. This is the project most like the one proposed, and the one the prices miss on the low side.
    • Lyon and Marseille, study estimates. Before risk the prices straddle what SNCF Réseau estimates for a deep four-track station with its tunnels: €3.5 billion against €3.8 billion for Lyon, €3.9 billion against €3.4 billion for Marseille, a figure that covers a whole phase of works. With risk, both are above the estimates, as a built cost tends to be: those estimates carry a contingency of their own, and in Paris such estimates have run 45% over.
    • Stuttgart, building. With 15% risk the prices land on the current forecast (€14.5 billion against €14.5 billion), which is in money of each year and would be higher in 2026 euros.
    • Zürich, built. The prices overshoot a final cost: €3.8 billion before risk against €2.8 billion. Zürich built a four-track station only 16 m down, under a working terminal, for half the Paris price per metre.
    • Munich, building. The prices give less than half the forecast (€4.8 billion with risk against €10.9 billion, which includes future inflation). Three stations 40 m under the centre are what a Paris project would look like if everything went wrong.
    The reading

    The prices are those of built projects, and the 15% is what separates the record's middle from its cheapest cases. It is not a cushion for an early estimate, because the prices already hold the overruns of the projects they come from. The spread between Zürich and Munich is the real uncertainty, and the RER E extension, the closest precedent, sits on the high side of the prices.

    The cost per year

    To compare a cost paid once with money and benefits that come every year, the construction cost is turned into a yearly repayment, like a loan repaid over 60 years at 3% above inflation. Money is spent for years before the first train runs: over 12 years of even spending assumption, interest during the works adds 20%. Each €1 billion of construction then costs €43 million a year.

    Running costs0.39
    Yearly cost2.19

    Running the tunnels and stations. Two French records exist. The first RER E section cost €21.3 million a year in 2003 to maintain and operate, for two deep stations and 4 km of tunnel; maintenance of the structures alone was six times the forecast.64 Brought to today with the public-works index, that is €13,200 a year per metre of platform track and about €3.5 million per km of tunnel. The RER network run by RATP costs more than €0.5 million per km of track to maintain, about €1.0 million per km of two-track tunnel.112 Stations are taken at the first figure and tunnels midway between the two, €2.25 million per km assumption. That gives €302 million a year, between €186 million and €358 million across the two records. What that does to the accounts is in the operations account.

    The State borrows long-term at 5.4% in October 2026, inflation included.113 The saving from closing the surface platforms and tracks is not deducted, because it has not been measured (study point I11). Running high-speed trains is left to their operators.

    Chapter 10

    How many more passengers

    The project would add about 13.1 million journeys a year on the TGV, the French high-speed train, and 31 million on suburban and regional trains. Most of the high-speed gain is between cities on two different lines: crossing Paris takes two or three changes of vehicle today, each of which turns passengers away, and a through train or a single change inside one station gives most of them back. The passenger charge falls only on these new uses, so no journey is lost against today: with it, 11.6 million high-speed journeys a year are added.

    What other cities saw

    Many cities have joined suburban lines through their centre and counted the passengers afterwards. For long-distance trains the record is thin: no railway has published its passengers before and after a terminal became a through station.

    • The best cases gained 24% to 30% within one to three years. Stockholm's commuter trains gained 26% in two years while the rest of the network gained 3%.122 Zürich gained 24% in the first year of its 1990 through station, with twice the trains.123 Tokyo's Fukutoshin line gained 30% in six months.121
    • Others gained little. Line E of the Paris RER, the express suburban lines that cross Paris underground, has gained about 10% so far on 30% more service.126 St. Gallen ran 25% more trains for 5% more travel.127 Philadelphia joined its two networks in 1984 during a collapse of service and saw no gain for ten years (unverified).128
    • Where a whole new line came with it, traffic multiplied, mostly by moving passengers. London's Elizabeth line joined two suburban services through a new tunnel: 56 million journeys on the two in 2019/20, 220 million in 2023/24 and 242 million in 2025/26.129 130 What made it different from a joined pair of terminal lines: new stations in the centre of the city, where the demand is, and far more trains, 24 an hour through the core. Only 9% to 10% of its journeys are new to public transport;131 in Sydney the figure is 27%.132 The annex on the Elizabeth line has the detail.

    Reading. A second stop in the city draws a real share of passengers, and removing a change of station is worth far more than the minutes it saves. But no case isolates the effect of a through station on long-distance traffic. That is why this study leans on British ticket data on changes, and on a model of time saved.

    Suburban and regional trains: 15% more on the joined lines

    In the plan, today's suburban lines become two through lines of the RER, each in its own tunnel. RER G (today's lines P and N) runs from the east under Nord-Est to Montparnasse and on to the south-west. RER F (today's lines H, K and L) runs from the north under Nord-Est to a new deep station under Saint-Lazare, and out onto the western suburban tracks; line L's branches become further branches of RER F. Line R stays on the surface at Gare de Lyon and does not run through; running it through is left as a later option (see the cost).

    Used here: 15% more journeys on the five suburban lines that run through (today's H, K, P, N and L) assumption. Line L, 77 million journeys a year, is counted with the 88% of its trains taken to run through the tunnel; the others still end at the surface station assumption. Line R gains nothing. The eight cases above average 16%, before deducting growth that would have come anyway. The 15% rests on the cases where lines were joined with little extra service, which is what this estimate assumes for Paris: the same trains, run through. On the 213 million journeys a year of the six lines, R included, that is 29 million more, of which 1.8 million are new trips from one suburb to another across Paris. The low and high cases take 5% and 25%: 11.0 and 47.9 million. Rebuilding the lines as through lines, with more frequent trains and a timetable across the region, is what gave the best cases their 24% to 30%; whether Paris would do that, and what it would bring, is study point I14 in what to verify.

    What the through lines are for. The point of RER G is not that riders from the east reach Montparnasse, which they can do today. It puts the residential north-east and east within one train of the research, university and company clusters of the south-west: Massy-Palaiseau, Saclay, Versailles, Saint-Quentin. The point of RER F is not Saint-Lazare, which line E of the RER already serves; it is a ride without a change from the northern suburbs to Clichy-Levallois, Pont-Cardinet, Courbevoie and La Défense, which relieves line E, full in the morning. Trips from one suburb to another across Paris are rare today because they are nearly impossible, not for want of demand; the Grand Paris Express line 15 was built on that same reasoning. The estimate here counts only the minutes saved to reach Paris and the suburb-to-suburb trips above; what these employment corridors bring beyond the stations is measured on the census in the economic return.

    • Regional express trains. No case exists for trains whose trips are long. The time model is used instead: traffic rises about 11% when the whole journey gets 10% shorter.88 The regional express trains run in the TGV tunnels, and all of them run through: those from the north run through Nord-Est to Montparnasse and on towards Chartres, Le Mans and Granville; those from the east run through Nord-Est to Gare de Lyon and on to Burgundy; those of Montparnasse and of Gare de Lyon run through to Nord-Est. A second stop saves them 1.8 to 4.1 weighted minutes on a trip taken as 100 minutes door to door assumption, which gives 4.0%, or 1.6 million journeys on 41 million. Gare de Lyon's regional trains, 5.2 million journeys a year, now go underground and gain 2.2 weighted minutes with Nord-Est as their second station. Of today's passengers, 22.1 million a year would get off at the second station and 2.8 million would cross Paris on the train, taken as 5% of today's users plus the gain from the change removed assumption (study point I15; see regional and suburban passengers).
    • A new journey is not always a new customer. Most of the growth seen elsewhere came from people who already used public transport. The financing chapter takes 30% of the extra suburban journeys as made by new holders of a Navigo pass, the travel pass of the region assumption: €21 million a year. New regional express passengers bring €13 million in fares. Together that is €34 million a year, a small sum (see more Navigo pass holders).
    • New lines take years to fill. Paris's RER D opened at 58% of its forecast and was at 84% eight years later; RER E opened at 53%.64 The figures here are for a mature service.

    High-speed trains: two gains, both counted cautiously

    Two groups of TGV passengers gain from the project, and each is estimated in its own way.

    Starting or ending in the Paris region

    102 million journeys a year today. With two stops in Paris for every train, the station where the train stops is nearer for most travellers: 5.9 minutes nearer on average, with walking and waiting counted at their official weights, to the station entrance (see reaching the station).

    The time model turns that into traffic: about 11% more for a journey 10% shorter.88 Result: 2.8 million more journeys, a gain of 2.8%. If the train’s ride between the two Paris stops were counted against the passenger, who then picks the train that calls at their best station, the saving would be 5.7 minutes and the gain 2.8 million; the central case does not count the ride, which a passenger on a long trip spends seated on the right train.

    Crossing Paris

    5.2 million journeys a year today (derived from the 2012-13 station survey, the last count made; a fresh one is study point I12, see crossing Paris). Each of them changes vehicle two or three times in Paris, from the TGV to the metro or the RER, sometimes from one metro line to another, then to the next TGV; only between Gare du Nord and Gare de l'Est is it a single change, on foot. With the project 47% of them stay on one train and the others change once, on the platforms of one station.

    Result: 10.3 million more journeys, 198% more than today, before the charge. Trains from London, Brussels, Amsterdam and Cologne can run on to the south like any other, since their passengers are checked before departure; northbound checks are open (study point I5).

    How the changes are counted. Each change of vehicle turns away part of the passengers who would otherwise make the trip: British ticket data find that an added change of train loses 37% of them in the long run.88 This study applies that loss to each change of a Paris crossing today assumption, so that a trip with two changes keeps 40% of its potential traffic and a trip with three, such as Gare de Lyon to Montparnasse by metro lines 1 and 4, keeps 25%. The number of changes for each pair of stations is read from the metro and RER map, by the route with the fewest assumption. A direct train gives the whole potential back. A passenger who still changes does so between two trains inside one station. Trains are not timed to meet, as in the Swiss pulse: each direction's trains are spaced evenly over the hour, so the wait for the next one is short. Such a change is counted as half a change assumption, the rule used here for suburban trips across Paris, and keeps 79% of the passengers. If it cost only what SBB, the Swiss railway, plans for a timed change, 12% less than a direct train,143 the gain would be 11.2 million journeys; if it cost a full change, 8.8 million. The shorter trip adds the time model on top: about 11% more travel for a trip 10% shorter, door to door.88

    What tempers it. The British loss was measured for one change of train inside a station, on routes of about 100 miles; applying it to every change of a Paris crossing is this study's reading, not a measurement. The one measurement made in Paris points lower: when the bypass line removed the change of station for trains between regions, their services carried 57% more than they would have without it (derived), new stations included.133 The low case therefore takes 37% on direct trains and the time model for the others: 1.5 million journeys. The high case puts every passenger of a served pair on a direct train: 12.2 million.

    The market the survey does not see. The 5.2 million are people who already cross Paris by train. The bypass line shows a wider market: its trains round Paris carried 21.9 million passengers in 2009, up from 10.2 million in 1999,18 and they are slow for the pairs that include the Atlantic line, 5h05 from Bordeaux to Lille against 4h27 with a change in Paris and 3h39 through Paris (SNCF's timetable, March 2026)2 assumption. Passengers who go by car or by air to avoid the change are not counted either. None of this is in the estimate, which applies the growth only to people who cross Paris by train today: study point I13.

    Destination by destination: time saved and traffic between cities

    Three main destinations are taken on each line: Lille, Brussels and London to the north; Strasbourg, Metz and Reims to the east; Lyon, Marseille and Montpellier to the south-east; Bordeaux, Nantes and Rennes on the Atlantic line. Their times from Paris are those of the fastest regular train (published timetables, unverified). Between two cities on different lines the trip today is the two train times plus 57.5 minutes from train to train in Paris (30 between Gare du Nord and Gare de l'Est). With the project it is the two train times plus the 20 minutes the train spends in Paris, two stops of 7 minutes and a run of 6, or plus a change of 12.5 minutes inside one station for those who change.

    The 54 pairs of cities: minutes today and with the project, and the growth of traffic
    • The changes matter more than the minutes. On a typical pair the trip gets 12% shorter, which alone would bring about 12% more travel. Removing two changes multiplies it by 2.5.
    • Atlantic to south-east gains most, because there is no metro line between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon and the crossing takes three changes today; the direct link removes all three. The growth here is applied only to people who change in Paris today, so those passengers are not counted again; whether some of them would move to the through trains is study point I13.

    Growth and supply: the estimate has none

    • The Atlantic line is short of seats. A new operator, Velvet, has ordered 12 trains to run between Paris and Bordeaux, Nantes, Rennes and Angers from 2028, and says it will add 10 million seats a year; by its own account 15% of would-be rail passengers go by car, coach or air for want of trains.19 The line to Lyon is being upgraded from 13 to 16 trains an hour each way by 2030.17
    • The central case holds traffic at today's level for the whole life of the project. The growth case lets it rise 1.5% a year: 127 million Paris-region TGV journeys a year instead of 104 million, 16.0 million added by the project instead of 13.1; the official reading of the economic return grows long-distance traffic 1.2% a year to 2070, as far as the busy-hour room allows. Traffic growth is study point I17.

    Capacity: what through platforms allow

    A terminal platform holds a train for 30 to 40 minutes while it is emptied, cleaned and refilled, once the margin kept behind it is counted (derived from a 20-minute planning figure and a 26-minute quickest turn-round);13 14 a through platform holds it for 7. Gare du Nord was turned down as the terminal of the airport express for lack of capacity.15 The new stations are sized for 29% more trains from the south than the standard hour assumed in this study (see how many platforms), and three tracks each way take 15 trains an hour: all of the Atlantic line's 15. Gare de Lyon has a fourth track each way, shared with the regional express trains, so the 16 planned on the south-east line fit too. Whether the platforms or the lines outside Paris cap the number of trains today is study point I1.

    If the platforms are the cap, each 10% of extra high-speed traffic would be 11 million journeys a year, about 1 times the gain counted in this chapter, and about €191 million a year of track charges for the railway. Whether it comes depends on the lines outside Paris and on demand, so it stays out of the central case; the sensitivity test with 10% more traffic is in what could change the answer.

    More journeys, and a charge that only new uses pay

    107millionhigh-speed journeys a year touch Paris102 million start or end there and 5.2 million cross it. Those who cross are counted at two stations, hence 112.5 million passengers counted at the four terminals (derived for 2024)84
    +12.2%high-speed journeys13.1 million more before any charge, 10.3 million of them across Paris
    +12%suburban and regional journeys31.1 million more on 253 million; 5% to 20% in the low and high cases

    About 107 million high-speed journeys a year touch Paris. The project changes how they begin, end or cross the city. For the 102 million that begin or end there, a station is a little nearer and few new journeys follow: 2.8 million. For the 5.2 million that cross it, two or three changes of vehicle disappear, and traffic between the cities of two lines grows 3.0 times: 10.3 million more journeys, 1.5 million in the low case that keeps the first estimate of this study.

    The financing of the project asks something only of those who use what it adds. The passenger charge tested there is €2.55 for boarding or leaving at a station the passenger's line did not serve before, and €5.10 for crossing Paris, on a direct train or with a change inside one station. Each line still stops at its own station at today's price, so a passenger from the Paris region pays only by choosing the other station, when it saves more time than the charge is worth: 38% of them would. A passenger who crosses Paris pays €5.10 against a gain worth about €50. Nobody pays more for the journey they make today, so no journey is lost; the charge only holds back part of the gain, 1.5 million journeys a year, which is why 11.6 million remain.

    What this means

    New high-speed traffic comes mostly from the cities that Paris now separates. It adds to the case without replacing its base: the time saved by people who already travel, worth about €866 million a year to high-speed passengers and €168 million to suburban and regional ones, the parks that replace the surface tracks and, outside this estimate, room for more trains later. The crossing estimate is also the least certain figure of this chapter: the economic return adds the benefits up, and what could change the answer tests each assumption, including the low case.

    Chapter 11

    Paying to run it, paying to build it

    The money is kept in two accounts. Running the tunnels and stations would cost about €386 million a year. A charge of €2.55 on high-speed passengers who use a station their line did not serve before, €5.10 on those who cross Paris, a like charge on regional express passengers, the track charges on the new journeys and the other income found here cover 189% of it, and between 166% and 271% across what running costs could turn out to be. Repaying construction costs €1.81 billion a year; the surplus of operations pays €0.35 billion of it, and the rest has to come from taxes and grants, as for most comparable tunnels.

    Two accounts

    Two words first: TGV is the French high-speed train, and RER the express suburban lines that cross Paris underground. An operations account holds what it costs each year to keep the tunnels and stations open, and what the project earns each year. A capital account holds the repayment of construction, spread over 60 years like a loan, and the taxes and grants assigned to it. Keeping them apart answers two different questions: can the project pay its own way once built, and who pays to build it.

    What the two accounts show

    The hope behind this split was that operations would pay for themselves and that the added economic activity would repay construction. The first holds, with room to spare: income covers 189% of running costs, 134% with no charge on any passenger, because the cities that Paris now separates bring 9.7 million new journeys a year across it and their track charges reach the project assumption. The surplus, €345 million a year, goes to the capital account. The second holds in value but not in cash: the benefits counted for the country are worth 142% of the yearly repayment of construction (see the economic return), but they are time, comfort, jobs and cleaner air and pass through no budget; what public budgets get back in taxes is a fraction of the repayment. The calculator shows what would have to change.

    The money chapters (financing, economic return) were checked by an independent reviewer on an earlier layout of the project; their figures for the present layout have not been checked again.
