    The running cost is the least certain figure

    Two French records exist, and they are far apart.

    • The first RER E section (two deep stations and 4 km of tunnel, opened in 1999) cost €21.3 million a year in 2003 to maintain and operate, several times its forecast: 8.7 for maintenance of the infrastructure, 9.2 for operating the stations, 3.4 for guarding and utilities.64 Brought to today with the public-works index, that is €13,200 a year per metre of platform track and about €3.5 million per km of tunnel. The index is a choice: no official index exists for running costs, and consumer prices have risen less.
    • The RER network run by RATP costs more than €0.5 million per km of track a year to maintain, so about €1.0 million per km of two-track tunnel.112
    • Used here: stations at the RER E rate; tunnels at €2.25 million per km, midway between the two assumption. The low case takes tunnels at the RER network rate and stations at 70% of the RER E rate; the high case takes both from the RER E record.
    • Gross, not net. The new stations replace terminals whose staff, cleaning and energy are paid for today. That saving is not deducted, because it has not been measured (study point I11). It would lower the cost again.
    • The level of the charge. Operations balance without any charge: with none on any passenger, income covers 134% of running costs, 117% at the high end of running costs. The charges then pay towards construction: doubling them to €5.10 and €10.20 would raise the surplus from €345 million to €421 million a year, and hold back 2.7 million new journeys instead of 1.5.
    • The weak point is the crossing traffic. In the low traffic case, which counts passengers who cross Paris on the lower estimate, income covers 100% of running costs. Most of the surplus rests on the cities of two lines travelling to each other as much as the changes removed suggest (see destination by destination).
    • What the package is worth. The regional express charge, the half share of the trainset saving and the shops together bring €125 million a year; shops at full yield would add €28 million more.
    • What to ask first. The track owner and the station operator hold the real running costs of RER E, of the stations opened in 2024 and of today's terminals. They decide whether this account balances.

    For comparison: fares cover 37% of the running of public transport in the Paris region (derived)146 and 64% in the Zürich network.147 The Elizabeth line earned £731 million in fares against £554 million of running costs in 2025 to 2026, trains included;130 it keeps its fares. Here the fares of high-speed trains belong to their operators and suburban fares to the region, which is why the project needs charges of its own.

    A charge on high-speed passengers who use what the project adds

    The proposal tested: nothing changes for a passenger who boards or leaves at the station of their own line, Gare de Lyon for the south-east, Montparnasse for the Atlantic coast, Nord-Est, entered from either historic hall, for the north and the east. Every train still stops there. A passenger who boards or leaves at another station, which their line did not serve before, pays €2.55, the price of a metro ticket in 2026.148 A passenger who crosses Paris pays €5.10, on a direct train or with a change inside one station. Each passenger can avoid the charge by doing what they do today, so the charge never makes a journey dearer than it is now.

    Who pays. A passenger from the Paris region uses the other station only when it saves more time than €2.55 is worth, about 4 minutes at the official value of time: 38% of them would, 40 million journeys a year, and they save 14 weighted minutes on average. All 14.9 million journeys across Paris pay, 8.2 million of them on a direct train.

    What it brings. €178 million a year: €101 million from the Paris region and €76 million from passengers who cross Paris.

    What it costs in traffic. No journey made today is lost, since none pays more than today. The charge only holds back part of what the project adds. In the Paris region, some passengers keep their own station when the other would save them only a few minutes, and the new journeys drawn by the time saved fall from 2.8 million to 1.9 million. Across Paris, €5.10 is 5.3% of two TGV fares; with French experts' response of traffic to fares, 0.7% fewer journeys for 1% more on the fare,149 the new journeys fall from 10.3 million to 9.7 million. With the charge, the project adds 11.6 million high-speed journeys a year instead of 13.1.

    Collecting it through the operators. The charge could also be billed to the train operators as a station charge per stop at the new stations and per train crossing Paris, rather than printed on each ticket. Operators would spread it across their fares as they see fit; passengers on the most sensitive fares would then see less of it, which is the case of a response of 0.5 rather than 0.7: 0.2 million more journeys a year. Both can be tried in the calculator.

    Is it possible in law? Two routes exist. Station charges are regulated at cost plus a return: €1,260 million a year for all French stations in 2026.150 The cost of the new stations would enter that base and be billed to train operators, who pass it on. European law also lets a track owner charge more for a specific project, on the basis of its long-term cost.151 The other route is a levy written into a budget law, as for the airport express, repaid in part by a levy on air passengers.152 153 Precedents for the level: the solidarity tax on a flight from Paris within Europe is €7.40;154 operators pay the Channel Tunnel about €35 per passenger (derived, upper bound).155 A charge that depends on the station used and on crossing Paris, not on every ticket, is a matter for the legal form chosen (study point I12). The figures here take the charge as free of VAT; if it carried the 10% VAT of tickets, the project would keep €2.32 of each €2.55.

    A charge on regional express passengers

    Regional express trains (TER) would run in the TGV tunnels, and every one of them would run through Paris. Northern TER would run through Nord-Est to Montparnasse and on to the Atlantic side, so their second station is Montparnasse; eastern TER would run through Nord-Est to Gare de Lyon and on to Burgundy, so their second station is Gare de Lyon; Atlantic TER and the TER of Gare de Lyon would run through to Nord-Est, their second station. Line R, a suburban line, stays on the surface at Gare de Lyon and pays nothing. The proposal tested: €2.55 for a passenger who gets off at the second station, the price of the metro ticket that passenger no longer buys;148 €5.10 for a passenger who crosses Paris without getting off. Nothing for a passenger who gets off at the first station, as today.

    Who paysPassengers a year, millionCharge€ million a yearWhere the number comes from
    Gets off at the second station22.1€2.555654% of today's 40.6 million regional express users, by line, from where in Paris they are going (see regional traffic)
    Crosses Paris without getting off2.78€5.10145% of today's users, plus the uplift on through journeys assumption. No count of these passengers exists (study point I15)
    Charge on regional express passengers7018% of the running cost
    • Why suburban trains carry nothing. About 47 million suburban passengers a year would also ride to the second station. Their Navigo pass or Île-de-France ticket already covers the metro ride they no longer make,148 so there is no saved fare to collect, and their gain is a few minutes, 3 to 8 depending on the line assumption. Regional express passengers from outside the region pay a separate metro fare today, and the charge replaces it.
    • No loss of traffic is modelled. The charge replaces a metro ticket at the same price, so the passenger's total fare does not rise assumption. It would be collected by the regional transport authority or the operator through the ticket, and paid to the project under an agreement.
    • Its weight. Without it, cover falls from 189% to 171%.

    More Navigo pass holders

    Navigo is the travel pass of the Paris region. Joining the suburban lines through Paris should bring new regular users: the model expects 29.5 million more suburban journeys a year (see regional traffic). A pass costs €998.80 a year whatever the number of trips,148 so a pass holder who travels more brings nothing. What counts is how many people buy a pass because of the project.

    The estimate. A regular commuter makes about 420 rail journeys a year assumption. If 30% of the new journeys are made by new pass holders assumption, that is about 21,100 passes and €21 million a year. The share is the unknown. Where it has been measured on new through lines, the share of journeys that are new to public transport was 9% to 10% in London,131 27% in Sydney (derived)132 and 28% to 32% on the East London line;156 the figure used here is at the top of that range.

    How to measure it. Count passes and validations on the joined lines before and after opening, RER F (today's lines H, K and L) and RER G (today's lines P and N), and compare with lines that did not change, such as line R, which is not joined. Passes are registered to a home address, so new holders along the joined lines can be counted directly. The regional authority's budget attributes no revenue to new lines today;146 an agreement would have to say that the measured gain is paid to the project.

    Its weight. Small either way. Fares bring the region €4.2 billion a year,146 and the project adds a few tens of millions at most. The extra running of the trains, €42 million a year, is charged to the project in the same account.

    The capital account

    Construction is paid once and repaid over 60 years. At 3% above inflation, with interest during 12 years of works, the €41.7 billion of construction costs €1.808 billion a year. Any shortfall of operations is added to it; a surplus goes to repay it. In the central case operations leave a surplus of €345 million a year.

The surplus of operations, €345 million a year, pays the rest, the same as €8.0 billion during the works. The grant alone understates the public share: it comes on top of a tax of €0.9 billion a year.
    • The business tax is a political choice, not a forecast. The existing one is committed to the Grand Paris Express until about 2071.167 It is counted here from the opening of the stations; collected during the works as well, as for the Grand Paris Express, it would bring more.

    Chapter 12

    What the country gets back

    This chapter answers six questions in order: what the project costs to build, what it costs and earns each year, what it gives back to the country, what the through trains change across France, how the money and the benefits run year by year, and how it compares with other projects. Benefits are valued with the official French method for transport projects, the rules the State applies to every new line,173 and each rule is named where it is used. Two readings are given side by side. The study's simple reading holds the benefits of the opening year flat against the yearly bill. The official reading values every year from the first works to 2140 and brings it all to today's money.

    The whole picture in six numbers

    €41.7bnTo buildPrices of 2026, with design, land and a 15% risk margin. €27.8bn at low unit prices, €62.0bn at high ones. See the cost chapter
    €1.81bn a yearTo repay constructionOver 60 years at 3%, interest during the 12 years of works included. This is the yearly cost of having built it
    €386m a yearTo runTunnels and stations €302m, the extra regional trains €42m, and €41m set aside each year to renew the rail systems. See the operations account
    €731m a yearEarned by the projectTrack charges and small charges on the new journeys, fees and shops. It covers the running costs 1.9 times; the €345m left over goes to the repayment. The other €1.46bn a year is public money
    €2.57bn a yearGiven back to the countryTime saved, the railway's own gains, comfort, access to jobs, a cleaner environment and the parks, at official values and today's traffic: 117% of the yearly bill of €2.19bn (repayment and running). Wider economic effects, €181m, are kept apart
    +€13.6bnNet value under the French rulesEvery year from 2028 to 2140 valued and brought to today's money at 4.5%: €0.45 of net gain for each euro invested, a return of 5.7% a year. +€17.6bn with the wider effects

    How to read this. The project pays for its own running with a surplus, but not for its construction: public money carries 81% of the capital, as it does for every new line in France. The question of this chapter is whether what the country gets back is worth that money. On the study's simple reading, the benefits of a single year cover 117% of the yearly bill. On the official reading, which lets traffic and the value of time grow over the life of the project, the country ends up €13.6bn ahead in today's money.

    Where the money goes, and where the value comes from

    Four charts, one question each: what the €41.7bn buys, where the project's own income comes from, who pays the yearly bill, and what makes up the benefits. Hover a slice for its figure.

    The benefits, one family at a time

    Nine families make up what the project gives back. Six come back every year and add up to €2.57bn at today's traffic: passengers' time, the railway's own gains, comfort and ease, access to jobs, the environment, and the parks. Two happen once: the land and savings the project frees, and the carbon of the works, counted against it. One grows with traffic: room for more trains in the busy hours. The last, wider economic effects, is reported apart, as the French method requires. Each card gives the value, how it is obtained in two sentences, and the official rules applied.

    1. Passengers' time

    €1,220m a year
    €25.8bn in today's money under the French rules measured

    TGV passengers from the Paris region reach a station nearer to them, 5.1 minutes closer on average on 102 million journeys a year, and the 5.2 million who cross Paris save 34 minutes and a change of station. Regional passengers reach the far side of Paris without a change, and regional express trains run through instead of ending at a terminal. Travellers between the west and the other regions, who ride a few slow bypass trains a day today, get an hourly through train by Paris, worth €138m a year; air passengers who take the train gain a little more.

    Official values of time: €35 an hour on long-distance trips, €31 on regional express, €15 in the Paris region; a minute spent walking, waiting or changing counts up to twice; new journeys count half.174 175 See the access map, crossing Paris and across France.

    2. The railway's own gains

    €605m a year
    €9.7bn in today's money official rule

    The new journeys pay tickets, and the French method counts what the railway keeps of them: the operator's margin and the track owner's charges, net of wear, €451m a year on the journeys through Paris and €40m on the cross-France journeys added. Trains that run through instead of waiting in a terminal free 17 TGV sets and 16 regional sets, €84m a year, and the surface terminals no longer need upkeep, €30m.

    Producers' balances are a required line of the French method.175 Margin 10% of the fare, track charges 35%, wear 15% of the charges. The part of these charges that the project itself collects is its income above, counted once.

    3. Comfort and ease

    €386m a year
    €8.1bn in today's money least firm

    A regular timetable: every direction leaves at the same minutes all day from a known platform, easy to remember, evenly spaced, and with a known place for each train after an incident, as in Switzerland. Passengers value such a timetable at 2.5 minutes a journey here, €164m a year on 113 million TGV journeys. Passengers who reach a station on the far side of Paris no longer ride the crowded metro legs in between, 69 million such trips a year, each crowded minute counting 1.40 minutes: €110m. Through platforms with a fixed track let the 51 million yearly departures arrive 2.5 minutes later at the station, €112m.

    A British survey of rail travellers values an hourly clockface timetable at 3.6 minutes a journey and even intervals at 4.6 to 8.6 minutes where trains run two to four times an hour;176 the Swiss railways carried 8.9% more passengers in the year their regular timetable was completed.177 1 to 5 minutes here. Crowding uses the official comfort factors for standing and seated passengers.174 178 The departure margin is an assumption of 0 to 5 minutes, see inside the station.

    4. Access to jobs across Paris

    €150m a year
    €3.5bn in today's money measured on census data

    The joined suburban lines put the northern suburbs within one ride of La Défense, Levallois and Courbevoie, and Meaux within one ride of Versailles and Saint-Quentin. Measured on the census commuting flows and the region's timetable, suburb to suburb trips by public transport across Paris rise from 146,000 to 229,000 a day, each saving 7 to 18 minutes with the official weights depending on the hub, at €15 an hour. The count holds homes and jobs where the census found them; as they move towards the better access, the gain rises by half over twenty years, to €370m in 2070.

    Fitted on 771,000 public transport commuters between suburbs, census 2022;179 180 the Grand Paris Express is in the reference. Details and the growth over the years in the job hubs. The wider effects of this access (denser job markets, people into work, better jobs) are reported apart, family 9.

    5. Environment

    €177m a year
    €1.8bn in today's money official values

    A quarter of the 13 million new TGV journeys replace a car trip: less carbon, €88m a year, and fewer accidents, less noise and pollution on the roads, €32m. About 383,000 air passengers a year take the through train once it matches the plane door to door, 94,000 tonnes of CO2 avoided, €40m. Closing the surface approaches to Gare du Nord and Gare de l'Est takes rail noise away from about 48,000 Parisians.

    Carbon at the official path, €491 a tonne in 2040 rising to €763 in 2050 (euros of 2015); road costs per car-km from the same fiche; in the official reading cars are carbon-free by 2050, which lowers the car part after that.174 181 182 183 184 The journeys and the flights are in across France.

    6. Parks, land and one-off savings

    €36m a year, and €0.42bn once
    €0.6bn in today's money assumption

    Three parks on the freed tracks, at Nord-Est, at Lyon-Bercy and at Montparnasse, about 87 hectares in all, three and a half times the Buttes-Chaumont: the largest parks made in Paris since the Second Empire. They draw about 8.7 million visits a year, valued with the health they bring at €40m a year less €4m of upkeep, and cost €0.31bn to clear and make. The small plots kept for building at their edges, 16 hectares, sell for €0.27bn, and the signal boxes of the surface approaches, due for renewal, are not renewed, €0.15bn.

    Of the 160 hectares of track fields read from maps, 109 are freed once the tracks the RER, line R and freight keep are taken out (82 to 136, never measured), 80% of them as parks. Visits as at the Buttes-Chaumont, 100,000 a hectare a year, 70% of them new; €3.3 a visit, the value a British tool gives an urban park visit, and as much again in health costs avoided, as London's account of its parks finds.185 186 187 188 189 190 191 The flats nearby gain value too, 0.7% for every 100 m nearer a park in Paris, a cross-check not added.192 See the parks.

    7. The carbon of the works, counted against the project

    -€0.57bn, once
    -€0.4bn in today's money assumption

    Digging 45 km of tunnels and four deep stations emits about 1.4 million tonnes of CO2, as the Grand Paris Express did per kilometre, valued at the official carbon price of each year of the works.

    Carbon 1.0 to 2.3 million tonnes.193 194 The disturbance of the works to today's trains, passengers and neighbours is not counted, as French appraisals do not count it: the Grand Paris Express evaluation carries no such line, and its reviewers asked for none.100 195

    8. Room for more trains in the busy hours

    €4.1bn in today's money
    Nothing in the opening year; grows with traffic assumption

    The terminals run 36 TGV paths an hour each way at the busy hours today and will manage 39.5 once planned works are done; the through stations allow 46. As long-distance traffic grows 1.2% a year, the journeys that today's terminals would turn away are valued at €20 each, half of them lost for good.

    This family only exists in the official reading, which lets traffic grow. Whether platforms are what limits trains is study point I1 (see the problem); without it the net value falls to +€9.5bn.

    Denser job markets make firms more productive, better access brings a few hundred people into work and lets others take better jobs, and TGV links widen the market of the cities joined. Each is measured with a published elasticity applied to this project's own traffic and journey times.

    The French method reports wider effects beside the net value, not inside it.175 Elasticities from the British guidance and the literature on high-speed lines.196 197 198 199 €2.0bn to €10.4bn.

    Not counted, on purpose

    • The travellers of the Lille to Lyon bypass trains. About 15 million passengers a year ride direct trains between the north and the south-east that avoid Paris by Roissy and Marne-la-Vallée. The through trains by Paris take 20 minutes longer, so these travellers keep their trains and gain a choice: counted at zero.
    • London trains running on to the south. Study point I5, not valued beyond the London air passengers who switch.
    • The disturbance of the works to today's trains, passengers and neighbours: left out, as French appraisals leave it out.100
    • Tax receipts. Counted apart in what public budgets get back, because the French method does not count them as a benefit.

    Across France without changing trains

    Today a TGV from the west ends at Montparnasse and one from the north at Gare du Nord: a traveller from Bordeaux to Lille crosses Paris by metro, 58 minutes from train to train, or takes one of the few direct trains a day that loop around Paris by Massy, an hour slower. With the project every train runs through Paris and on, with two stops of a few minutes: Lille to Bordeaux in instead of , Bordeaux to Strasbourg in , Rennes to Strasbourg in , Lille to Marseille, the two cities furthest apart, in , every hour. The plane, airports included, takes about as long door to door, which is where rail wins the market.200

    Rail times from SNCF's timetable for a weekday of March 2026: today with a change of station in Paris, the connections a traveller would choose; with the project, the same trains' runs plus 20 minutes through Paris.2 By air: 150 minutes to reach the airport, check in, board, leave and reach town, plus the flight assumption. Air passengers of 2025 between the two cities.182 Rail's share of rail and air from the published curve: about 90% at two hours, 70% at three, 55% at four, 35% at five.200

    Who gains, and what is counted

    • The 5.2 million who change station in Paris today stay on their train: family 1, the largest item of the count, with the journeys the change held back.
    • The travellers of today's bypass trains. 21.9 million passengers a year rode direct trains between two regions in 2009, 17.6 million of them on routes through the Paris region, scaled here by the growth of TGV traffic since.18 201 Those between the north and the south-east keep their direct trains (counted at zero). The 3.5 million between the west and the other regions have two to four slow trains a day today, by Massy; the project gives them an hourly train, up to 55 minutes faster: €138m a year, and 753,000 new journeys.
    • Air passengers. 213,000 a year between French cities and 170,000 from London switch to the train. They gain €6m, the railway keeps €40m of the new fares, and the flights not flown save 94,000 tonnes of CO2 a year, €40m at the official carbon value.182 202 183

    Why the carbon figure stays modest

    Air travel between the French regions is small: 8.2 million passengers in 2025, most of them to Nice and Toulouse, which stay beyond five hours by train even with the project, and the pairs the project puts under four hours carry a few hundred thousand each.182 The larger lever is the car, which carries most long-distance trips in France: a quarter of the new journeys counted in the model come from it, €88m of carbon a year in family 5, and the official scenario makes cars carbon-free by 2050, after which the saving is on accidents, noise and congestion only.181

    What the table shows is the other half of the story: for weekends and holidays, millions of people in the regions gain a direct train every hour to regions they could only reach by changing in Paris. The count values that choice through the journeys it adds; it values nothing for the travellers who already had a direct train.

    The job hubs the joined suburban lines reach

    Lines H, K and L become one line, RER F, from the northern suburbs through Gare du Nord to Saint-Lazare and the north-west; lines P and N become another, RER G, from Meaux through Paris to Versailles and Saint-Quentin. The question is how many commuters that helps, and the answer was measured rather than assumed: the census gives every home to work flow by commune and by mode,179 and the region's timetable gives the door to door time of each pair with and without the project, the Grand Paris Express included in both.180 Trips respond to the time saved with the elasticity found for the Elizabeth line and in the literature.203 199

    How the gain grows over the years

    The count holds homes and jobs where the 2022 census found them. Firms and households move towards better access over fifteen to twenty years: the Grand Paris Express appraisal models that move and its reviewers note that the location effects are not complete at opening and keep rising to 2035.100 Here the commuters' gain rises by half over twenty years in the central case, nothing in the low case, double in the high case, on top of the official growth of trips and of the value of time: €175m in 2040, €330m in 2060, €370m in 2070, then flat.

    The money and the benefits, year by year

    The returns grow with time while the cost is paid first, so the shape of the years matters as much as the totals. Three charts: what is spent and earned each year, what the country gets back each year against what it costs, and the running total in today's money, which says when the project has paid itself back for society.

    How the French rules were applied

    France evaluates every transport project with one method, set by an instruction of 2014 and a set of technical fiches of the Ministry of Transport.173 175 Its headline figure is a net present value: every cost and benefit of every year, brought to today's money with a discount rate, costs subtracted. The table says what each rule is, the value used here, and where on this page it applies. The study's own simple reading is kept beside it because it needs no forecast: it asks whether one year's benefits at today's traffic cover one year's bill.

    What public budgets get back

    The French method does not count taxes as a benefit, so this is a view for public finances beside the appraisal, not inside it. Added activity pays taxes, and part of the public money spent returns to public budgets. Three layers must be kept apart because they do not have the same standing, and the answer depends on one question this study cannot settle: how much of the activity added around the stations is new for the country, and how much is moved from elsewhere.

    • Layer 1: money that reaches the Treasury because of the project. Tickets carry 10% VAT, which businesses cannot recover.209 It applies to the ticket money of the new journeys: €97 million a year in the central case. VAT lost on what passengers stop buying elsewhere is not deducted. Experience elsewhere is that this layer can be negative: the evaluation of High Speed 1 found a loss of tax of over £0.8 billion, because rail travel is taxed less than what it replaces.170
    • Layer 2: tax on added activity. France takes 43.6% of its output in taxes and social contributions.210 What is in doubt is how much of a local gain is new for the country. British guidance starts from the assumption that none is, unless the project is shown to bring more people into work:211 212 the first column. The middle column takes the wider effects as the appraisal of the Grand Paris Express counts them: each extra job is valued at €10,000 a year of unemployment benefits saved,100 and output from denser job markets and from working time saved (for the 30% of TGV passengers who travel for work, unverified213) is taxed at 43.6%. The last column supposes that the 18,500 jobs implied are all new and each pays tax on the average output of a job in the region, €123,220.214
    • Layer 3: tax returned by the works. A simulation by the French economic observatory finds that 40% to 60% of debt-financed public investment returns to public budgets within five years, through wages, profits and lower benefits.215 It is not a gain from this project: any spending of the same size would return the same.
    How official appraisal treats taxes

    The French method counts each euro of public money at €1.20 because raising taxes has a cost of its own, and it leaves out jobs created by the works and multiplier effects to avoid counting twice.216 205 The builder of the Grand Paris Express claimed up to €4 billion of tax a year; the State's reviewers did not endorse a tax line.217 100 For Crossrail, consultants put tax at 27% to 29% of added output.218

    The reading. Between nothing and about €1,220 million a year comes back, €420 million on the middle reading: 23% of the yearly repayment of construction, 68% on the most generous reading. Tax receipts lower the net cost for public budgets; on no reading do they repay construction.

    Against comparable projects in France and abroad

    The measure used everywhere is the ratio of benefits to costs over the life of the project, both brought to today's money. Above 1, the country gets back more than it spends. Under the French rules this project stands at 1.34 on the benefits counted and 1.44 with the wider effects, directly comparable with the French appraisals of the Grand Paris Express and the Marseille tunnel, which use the same rate and horizon. The others are not strictly comparable, and the differences cut both ways:

    • French appraisals use 4.5%, count effects to 2140 and weigh public money at 1.2: the basis of this project's 1.34. The study's simple reading, at 3% with benefits held flat, gives 1.17, and 1.26 with the wider effects.
    • British appraisals deduct ticket revenue from the cost, which raises the ratio. The Elizabeth line's 1.97 becomes about 0.8 to 1.2 on gross cost, derived from its published present values.219
    • Australian appraisals use a 7% rate, which lowers theirs.220

    What the comparison says

    • On transport benefits alone, cross-city tunnels rarely return much more than their cost. Published ratios at approval run from about 0.5 to 2. Five of the thirteen stand below 1 on those benefits; they were built or are promoted for capacity, or rest on wider effects: Stockholm, Malmö, Gothenburg, Lucerne, the Grand Paris Express.
    • Wider effects decide the largest projects. They are a fifth to a third of the benefits in London, Sydney and Melbourne, and about 60% for the Grand Paris Express. Here they are 7% of the benefits, because they are measured on this project's own flows rather than taken as a ratio.
    • Measured returns are usually lower than forecast. High Speed 1 went from 1.5 to 0.64, Stockholm from 0.86 to 0.51, RER E from 21% to about 10%.
    • Per passenger, the cost is in the range of the others. About €152 of capital for each yearly journey, against about €150 for the Elizabeth line and about €210 for Lucerne (derived). Paris already has five RER lines through its centre, so the project does not open a crossing that did not exist: it joins the long-distance network to it.
    • Where this project stands. At 1.34 under the French rules it is level with Munich, Melbourne and Frankfurt at approval and above the Grand Paris Express on transport benefits; with wider effects, at 1.44, it is below the Grand Paris Express, Sydney and London, whose wider effects are larger ratios. Most of its benefits are measured on its own traffic; the least firm, the departure margin, the regular timetable and the room in the busy hours, are tested in the next section.

    What could change the answer

    Each bar changes one thing in the official reading and shows the net present value that results; the tick is the central case. Three questions matter more than all the others: the construction price, whether traffic grows, and whether the railway's own gains and the room for more trains are counted as the method says.

    Growth and room overlap

    Benefits can only grow 1.2% a year for thirty years if the trains can carry the passengers. The growth in the official reading therefore needs the room that the project is meant to unlock: the busy-hour room of family 8 is the condition of the growth, not a benefit on top of it, which is why it is valued only on the journeys the terminals would turn away.

    What would settle the largest open points, and who can:

    1. Room for more trains (study point I1). The count values the journeys the terminals would turn away at €20 each. The view of the track owner, SNCF Réseau, of when each terminal and each line is full, with and without the project, would replace that assumption. Without any value for room the net value is +€9.5bn; at €40 a journey it is +€16.6bn.
    2. The regional network (I14). The job-access count is measured on the census and the timetable; a run of the region's own travel model would confirm it, show the relief of the RER and give a figure of its own for the wider effects.
    3. The parks and the land (I19). About 87 hectares of parks and 16 of building plots are counted, on areas read from plans; a survey of the track fields would settle the hectares, and a decision of the City what is built and how many visits the parks can expect.

    The construction price, traffic and running costs can also be moved by hand in the financing calculator.

    Chapter 13

    What could change the answer, and what to verify

    The case rests on a handful of things nobody has yet measured or drawn. Cost and the time needed to board in a deep station move the economic result most; the traffic that crosses Paris, more than running costs, decides how far the project pays its way once open. Most of these can be settled by studies that cost little next to the project, and twenty-seven study points are listed at the end. Running regional express trains in the TGV tunnels rests on one condition: signalling that lets trains follow each other about 1.5 minutes apart. Line R at Gare de Lyon stays on the surface; running it through is left as a later option.

    How sure is the result?

    Each line changes one assumption of the station model and shows the share of the yearly cost that the benefits counted then cover: the complete count of the economic return, held flat at today's traffic. The central case is 117%. The official reading, with growth and the French rules, has its own tests in what could change the answer. The one test that changes only the project's income, 10% more TGV traffic once the platforms no longer cap the lines, is left out of the chart and shown in the financing chapter; the room for more trains is valued in the official reading only, as the journeys the terminals would turn away (see what could change the answer).

    • Cost matters most. The same benefits cover 83% to 163% of the cost depending on prices and risk.
    • Boarding time comes next. Two minutes more for every passenger removes 21% of the benefits: an extra 2.9 minutes on the clock is enough to cancel the whole gain in access. This is why the design of the Nord-Est station is the first thing to study (see inside the station).
    • How access is counted matters less. TGV passengers are counted at the station entrance. If the train’s ride between its Paris stops were counted against them, even with each passenger picking the train that calls at their best station, benefits would cover 117% of the cost assumption, study point I16.
    • Growth over time counts. Benefits are held flat in this chart. The official reading lets long-distance traffic grow 1.2% a year and the value of time 0.8% to 2070: +€13.6bn net in today's money, while the official stress test with no growth at a 4% rate gives a negative value of €5.0bn (see what could change the answer); growth needs the capacity the project is meant to unlock.
    • The employment corridors are counted on the census. Commuters who gain a through suburban line across Paris, mainly from the northern suburbs to La Défense, Courbevoie and Levallois and from Meaux to Versailles and Saint-Quentin, are worth €150m a year at opening, rising as homes and jobs move towards the access; the region's travel model would confirm it (study point I14).
    • The money side has its own tests. Running costs, the level of the charges and the response of passengers to them are tested in the operations account and can be moved in the calculator.

    RER F under the 9th arrondissementThe tunnel from Nord-Est to Saint-Lazare, 2.6 km with its curve, and its return to the surface on the Batignolles tracks, 1.2 km, are read from maps. RER E's tunnel from Magenta to Haussmann-Saint-Lazare, on a similar line, is about 2.46 km (unverified). The deep station under Saint-Lazare has no design and no hall cost.The stationsI24
    Line R at Gare de LyonGare de Lyon's regional express trains, Bercy's included, go underground on the fourth track each way and run through to Nord-Est: that part is settled. Line R stays on the surface on a small terminal. Running it through to an eastern line would need 2 more tracks at Gare de Lyon and 2 at Nord-Est, 330 m long, about €2.1 billion all-in, for 5 trains an hour with no proven partner demand (the partner would be extra line P trains towards Meaux or Provins). It is left as a later option.Today's stationsI21
    Regional express trains in the TGV tunnelsThe tunnels are planned on paths 2 minutes apart, 30 an hour each way: TGVs keep their places of the 12-minute beat and the regional express trains take the paths between them. That needs signalling for trains about 1.5 minutes apart, ETCS level 2 with short blocks and automatic driving in the tunnels assumption. Planners keep the peak under 75% of capacity. The busiest tunnel is the Atlantic approach, 15 TGVs and 11 regional express trains an hour: 65% of capacity at 1.5 minutes, 87% if signalling only reaches 2. In that case the regional express trains would need their own tunnel to Vanves, 2.8 km, about €0.9 billion all-in, not in the estimate. The next limit is the regional express platforms at Nord-Est, used 88% of the hour.How the trains are pairedI27
    London trainsNo tracks are sealed: one of the six TGV tracks at Nord-Est is closed off for each London departure, with a larger control hall above (€0.2bn assumption), as Amsterdam does from one platform.28 Arrivals need no check. The open point is northbound: passengers boarding in a southern station for London must be checked before boarding.PlatformsI5
    CDG Express at Gare de l'EstThe airport express is planned to leave from Gare de l'Est on surface tracks.153 If the surface halls close, it needs a place in the Nord-Est station or another terminal.Today's stationsI6
    Building under five live stationsStuttgart's through station is now due in 2031 at €14.5 billion.82 The RER E extension ran 45% over.72 Each year added to the works adds about 1.5% to the cost through interest; 15 years instead of 12 lowers the cover from 117% to 113%.How it would be builtI8, I10
    Protected buildingsGare du Nord, Gare de l'Est and Gare de Lyon are listed.29Today's stationsI19
    Parks instead of salesThe track areas of Gare du Nord, Gare de l'Est and Montparnasse are freed entirely and become parks: about 87 hectares of parks on the 160 hectares of track fields with the Gare de Lyon site, and 16 hectares of small building plots; no land is sold in the accounts. At Gare du Nord and Gare de l'Est this is why every line goes underground: one line left on the surface would keep the cost and lose the park. At Gare de Lyon the regional express tracks and the Bercy station are freed too; line R keeps a few surface tracks. Against a sale of the land, this raises the public grant by about €2 billion to €3 billion assumption; the plots sold once, €0.27bn, and the €0.31bn to clear and make the parks are counted in the economic return, not in the construction cost. Both need a decision.The parksI19
    15% risk may be judged thin by reviewersThe unit prices come from final costs and signed contracts, so they already hold past overruns, and the back-test against seven projects supports 15%. Reviewers used to 30% or more on early estimates may not accept it; at 30% with high prices the cost is €62 billion.The back-testI10
    Delays spreading between branchesJoined lines share their incidents; the count gives no value to the reliability of the joined suburban lines, and values the regular timetable of the TGVs as an assumption with a range.The benefitsI14
    Taxes that are already spoken forThe tax on businesses that repays the Grand Paris Express runs to about 2071.167 A second one of the same size is a political choice, and the grant on top of it is €12 billion, 29% of the cost.The capital accountI20

    Stages and the decision

    The project can be built in two stages: first the TGV part of Paris Nord-Est and Gare de Lyon, with its eight tracks, the north, east and south-east TGV tunnels and the tunnel between the two stations, together with RER F from the north through Nord-Est to Saint-Lazare and most of the links that bring regional express trains into the TGV tunnels, 19.2 km of twin-track tunnel for €22.4 billion all-in; then Montparnasse, with the TGV tunnels to Nord-Est and the Atlantic, the direct link, RER G and the regional express platforms at Nord-Est, 25.3 km for €19.3 billion; see works and stages. The first stage serves the trains of three of the four high-speed lines and the northern suburban lines. Its benefits on its own have not been estimated, so this study cannot say whether stopping after it would be a better or a worse project, and the staging itself is study point I8: the order, what each stage leaves usable, and whether the link can wait.

    What to decide now

    Not whether to build. The decision today is whether to spend on seven quick tests that can confirm or stop the case:

    1. Ask for ticket data on passengers who change station in Paris, by origin and destination (study point I12).
    2. Draw one standard hour of trains with the track owner (SNCF Réseau): every TGV stopping at two of the three stations, six tracks a station, no train reversing (I2, I3).
    3. Commission a concept design of the Nord-Est station with its 20 tracks (6 TGV, 4 regional express, 10 suburban): position, depth, time from hall to train, and a first engineer's price (I2, I9).
    4. Ask what deep stations and tunnels cost to run, from the records of RER E and of the stations opened in 2024, net of what today's terminals cost (I11). How large the surplus of operations is turns on it.
    5. Ask when each terminal and each line is full, with and without the project (I1). The official reading values the room for more trains at €20 a journey the terminals would turn away, €4.1bn in today's money, an assumption; the view of the track owner would replace it.
    6. Run the region's travel model on the two through suburban lines, RER F and RER G: suburb to suburb trips, the jobs within reach along each corridor, relief of RER E, frequency (I14, I26).
    7. Measure the parks: a survey of the track fields, and a decision of the City on what is built and how many visits the parks can expect (I19); and decide whether line R should later run through (I21).
    8. Ask the track owner whether the TGV tunnels can be signalled for trains about 1.5 minutes apart, with ETCS level 2, short blocks and automatic driving (I27). The regional express trains in the TGV tunnels depend on it.

    With those in hand, settle the level and the legal form of the passenger charges (I12, I15), fix the stages (I8), and take the case to a full appraisal.

    The case in three sentences
    • Operations pay for themselves and leave a surplus. With €2.55 on TGV passengers who use a station their line did not serve, €5.10 on those who cross Paris, the same on regional express passengers who use the second station, the track charges on new journeys and half of the operators' saving on trainsets, income covers 189% of running costs (166% to 271% across the running-cost range, 100% in the low traffic case).
    • Construction needs public money for most of its cost. The benefits counted are worth 117% of the yearly cost, and +€13.6bn net in today's money under the French rules, but they pass through no budget; a business tax package, a European grant and a grant of €12 billion add up to 81% of the €41.7 billion.
    • The judgement rests on the least firm items. Most of the benefits are measured on the project's own traffic; the room for more trains in the busy hours, the regular timetable and the later arrival at through platforms are assumptions with ranges. Without any one of them the net value stays positive (+€9.5bn, +€9.9bn and +€11.1bn), and the uncertain items together take it from +€4.4bn to +€25.2bn.

    Annex A

    Zürich: a terminus that became a through station

    Zürich's main station was a terminus: 16 tracks ending at buffer stops in the middle of the city. Rather than enlarge it, the canton twice built a four-track through station underneath, in 1990 and in 2014, each with its own tunnel. The eight through tracks are under a third of the station's platform tracks and carry, on a rough count, close to half of its trains.

    Four stations in one

    Zürich Hauptbahnhof is four stations on one site: the surface hall, two underground through stations on its north and south edges, and a small terminus for two local lines under the forecourt. A level of passages and shops ties them together. The S-Bahn, named throughout, is the suburban rail network of the Zürich region. Choose a year to see the station grow, and a part to read what it is, when it opened, what it cost and which trains use it.

    Parts of the station

    The hall

    • What: 16 dead-end tracks on the surface, numbered 3 to 18, under a train shed of 1933, with seven island platforms and two side platforms.234 Track 3 is the southern edge and track 18 the northern edge.235
    • Platforms: lengthened to 420 m in 2002 to 2004.67
    • Trains: long-distance trains that end here or turn back, international trains and four S-Bahn lines.236 About 18 of the 27 long-distance departures in one hour of 2026 (derived).12
    • Before 1989: the tracks were numbered 1 to 16.234

    Passages and shops

    • What: four passages run north to south under the hall tracks. Three of them form one complex with the shops under the forecourt.236 Its two halls lie 4.7 m and 7.3 m below ground.234
    • Dates: first shops in 1970, enlarged in 1990 and 2014.234 The westernmost passage was widened from about 10 m to about 35 m in 2005 to 2008, with a lift and escalators to each platform, for CHF 56.8 million.68 237
    • Why it matters: the passages join both underground stations to each other and to the hall.10 The station's standard minimum time for a change is 7 minutes.238

    The river Sihl

    • What: the river crosses the station under the tracks in five culverts about 190 m long, each about 12 m wide and 3 m high. The bridges that carry the 16 tracks are the roof of the culverts.239
    • Under it: the roof of Löwenstrasse station lies about 1 m below the river bed,239 and its tracks 11 m below the river.68
    • During the works: two of the five culverts were dried at a time, in four stages from April 2008 to December 2010, while the river ran in the other three. The site was to be cleared and flooded if a large flood was forecast.68

    Museumstrasse station

    • What: four through tracks, 41 to 44, on two island platforms 360 m long, 13.6 m below the street of the same name on the north side.234
    • Opened: May 1989 for a few regional trains,234 and 27 May 1990 for the S-Bahn.240
    • Trains: S-Bahn only, 11 lines.236 Up to 20 trains an hour each way at the peak.123 Stadelhofen, the next station on the same lines, sees 770 trains a day.241
    • Cost: part of the line of 1990, CHF 866 million in all.242

    Tunnels to the east

    • What: the Hirschengraben tunnel, 2.1 km underground of which 1.3 km bored, leads to Stadelhofen station; the Zürichberg tunnel, 5.0 km, carries on to the suburbs.243 244 About 12 km of new line in all.123
    • Opened: 27 May 1990, after nine years of works.240
    • Cost: CHF 866 million with Museumstrasse station, of which the canton paid 80%.242
    • Today's limit: Stadelhofen has three tracks and is described as the largest bottleneck of the S-Bahn. A fourth track with second tunnel tubes is planned for 2027 to 2037 at CHF 1.1 billion.241

    SZU terminus

    • What: two dead-end tracks, 21 and 22, with one island platform 125 m long, 11.6 m below the forecourt.234 SZU is a separate local railway.
    • Opened: 5 May 1990. It uses a section built ahead for an underground railway that voters rejected in 1973.245 246
    • Cost: a credit of CHF 72.4 million, approved by 67% of voters in 1983.246
    • Trains: two local lines, to the Sihl valley and to the Uetliberg, about seven trains an hour.245

    Sihlpost wing station

    • What: four extra dead-end tracks, 51 to 54, on the surface south of track 3 and set back from the hall. In service from 2003, closed on 15 June 2014 and removed.235
    • Trains: the S-Bahn lines S1, S2, S8 and S14, which turned back here.247
    • Why: it freed hall tracks for the national timetable of 2004. The government accepted it only as an unavoidable stopgap: it met broad opposition because of longer changes and worse access to the city centre.247

    Löwenstrasse station

    • What: four through tracks, 31 to 34, on two island platforms 420 m long and 13.5 m wide, 16 m below hall tracks 4 to 9.10 67 The whole structure is 675 m long.10
    • Opened: 15 June 2014 for the S-Bahn, 13 December 2015 for long-distance trains.248 249
    • Cost: CHF 674 million for the station.101
    • Trains: 460 a day, of which 140 long-distance and 320 S-Bahn.10 In 2026: four Intercity lines between western and eastern Switzerland, one regional express and the trains to Munich.12
    • Built under the working hall: its roof and walls were laid in 2002 to 2004, when the platforms above were being rebuilt anyway.68 See the lessons.

    Weinberg tunnel

    • What: 4.8 km, two tracks in one tube more than 11 m across, from the east end of Löwenstrasse station to Oerlikon.10 It passes under the river Limmat and 5 m below the Hirschengraben tunnel, then turns through about 180 degrees to reach Oerlikon from the south.250
    • Built: main drive from June 2010, breakthrough on 22 November 2010.251 Opened with the station on 15 June 2014.248
    • Cost: CHF 498 million.101
    • Trains: 12 S-Bahn trains an hour each way at opening.248 Main station to airport in 9 minutes by Intercity.252

    Bridges to the west

    • What: two bridges, 1,156 m and 394 m long, carry the new line in from Altstetten, to the west.10 A ramp leads down to the station; the approaches slope at up to 37 mm per metre.251
    • Opened: December 2015. Long-distance trains have run through the station since then.10 249
    • The whole line: 9.6 km from Altstetten to Oerlikon.253

    Details cited to Wikipedia in these descriptions are unverified: the layout of the hall and the lines that use each part, the sizes and depths of Museumstrasse station and of the SZU terminus, the levels and dates of the passages, the lengths and route of the tunnels, the figures for Stadelhofen, the dates of the wing station and the vote of 1983.

    Why through platforms, and not a bigger terminus

    Twice the first plan was something else, and twice voters chose a through station by a large majority.

    YearWhat happened
    1973Voters reject a credit of CHF 599 million for an underground railway with an S-Bahn: 57% no.246
    1981They approve CHF 523 million for the S-Bahn alone, with a through station under the north edge of the main station: 74% yes.246 242
    1990The line opens after nine years of works.240 On a working day, S-Bahn traffic at the city boundary is 24% higher in the first year.123
    1990sFor the national timetable of 2004, the railway plans a wing station beside the hall for four S-Bahn lines, and two more tracks on the viaduct towards Oerlikon: about CHF 650 million, plus CHF 200 million to CHF 300 million further out.254 255
    1997 to 1998Residents of two city districts resist the wider viaduct, and the canton's heritage and noise offices oppose it.67 256
    1999A popular initiative, "For a through station, no wing station", asks for a tunnel and an underground through station. The government answers with a proposal of its own and the initiative is withdrawn.257
    2001Over 80% of the canton's voters (82% in the engineering press) approve CHF 580 million, the canton's 40% share of an estimate of CHF 1,450 million.237 69 257
    2003The wing station opens all the same, as a stopgap, and closes the day the through station opens in 2014.235

    The vote shares of 1973 and 1981 and the dates of the wing station are from Wikipedia and unverified; the canton confirms the date and the amount of the vote of 1981.

    The reasons given at the time were not journey times first.

    1. The terminus could not grow where it stood. The government found the scope to develop the station at its site and level "severely limited". A new main station on another site was examined and dropped.247
    2. The bottleneck was the line out, not only the platforms. Towards Oerlikon and the airport, more trains were "hardly possible". A through station joined to a new pair of tracks was called "the key element".247
    3. The wing station put passengers too far from their connections. The initiative called the walk from there to the express trains unacceptable; a through station under the hall gives "the most direct connections to the other tracks".247
    4. Turning back wastes platforms and tracks. The trade press called it "a time waster" and an "inefficient use of platform and track space".258 The canton listed the end of the reversal among the gains.259
    5. It was built for long trains from the start. The canton judged that the S-Bahn alone would never fill a second through station. Platforms of 420 m instead of 300 m cost just under CHF 30 million more.247

    The result, as stated by the engineers: four through tracks raised the capacity of the whole station by about one third.67 The gain was not published in trains per hour.

    How to read it. A through train that waits for connections still stands 6 to 9 minutes. Only a train that does not wait shows the bare stop of 3 minutes, and a train that turns back can leave after 5. So the length of the stop is set mainly by the connections, not by the reversal (derived). What the through station removes is the reversal itself, the crossing of other trains' paths on the way in and out, and several minutes of approach. Where a locomotive must be changed at a reversal, that alone takes 4.5 minutes.238

    The benchmark for Paris. The four through tracks of Löwenstrasse take about 460 trains a day,10 about 6 per track an hour on average over a service day of 19 to 20 hours (derived). The rule used for the Paris stations sizes a high-speed track at 5 trains an hour: a stop of 7 minutes, 2 minutes held for a late train and 3 minutes between a departure and the next arrival, a place of 12 minutes assumption. With the lines full, the six high-speed tracks at Nord-Est and at Montparnasse are loaded at 4.3 and 5.0 trains an hour per track, and the eight at Gare de Lyon at 4.0, whose fourth track each way also takes the regional express trains: see how many platforms. The two counts are not quite alike. Zürich mixes long-distance and suburban trains on the same four tracks, and its trains bunch around the hour; Paris gives regional express trains their own platforms, except on the fourth track each way at Gare de Lyon, and spreads the stops through the hour.

    What changed

    1 in 3long-distance trains runs through9 of 27 departures and 8 of 25 arrivals in one hour of 2026 (derived)12 11

    Traffic. The first through station changed the S-Bahn most. On a working day, 159,288 passengers crossed the city boundary by S-Bahn in the year before it opened, 196,854 in the first year after, and 445,562 in November 2014: 180% more in 24 years, with twice as many trains an hour at the peak.123 From 2014 to 2019, with the second through station, S-Bahn traffic grew by a further 19%.124 How much of this growth is due to the stations themselves cannot be separated from the growth of the region and of the service.

    Trains. The station handled about 1,400 trains a day around 2000 and about 2,000 in 2007.264 65 Around 2020 it handled 2,915 train movements a day, of which 2,607 passenger trains (unverified).235

    Journeys. S-Bahn trains cross the city about 6 minutes faster and long-distance trains up to 7 minutes faster; the main station is 9 minutes from the airport.248 265 252 A few journeys became longer.

    Cost. The line of 1990 cost CHF 866 million in the final account. The canton paid CHF 693 million, 80% of it: CHF 14 million less than its credit of CHF 523 million once CHF 69 million of approved extra works and CHF 114 million of inflation were added.242 The cross-city line of 2014 and 2015 was put to voters at CHF 1,450 million at 2000 prices.257 Its final account is CHF 2,052 million at 2005 prices, 1% above the ceiling of CHF 2,031 million agreed in 2008; the canton paid one third and the Confederation two thirds.101 In this study's 2026 euros the line comes to about €2.75 billion.

    Punctuality: no figure is published for Zürich before and after the through stations. The regional transport authority states that the main station now has enough capacity for the growth expected in the foreseeable future and that timetable stability improved across Switzerland.10

    What Paris can take from it, and where the comparison stops

    What carries over

    • Put the through tracks where the trains already are. Both new stations lie under the old hall or right beside it, and one level of passages serves all of them. The wing station beside the hall was accepted only as a stopgap, because of the walk.
    • A few through tracks do a lot. Four of them added about a third to the capacity of the whole station.67
    • Build for long trains at once. Platforms of 420 m were a small extra cost, and they are why Intercity trains use the station today.
    • It can be built under a working station. The roof slab, walls and columns went in first, from the surface; the station was then dug out under the slab. Normally two hall tracks at a time (two to three in the engineering press) were shortened by 100 m, leaving about 300 m of platform in use, and trains kept running on all the other tracks.66 67 The listed south wing of the station building was underpinned and settled by 10 to 15 mm, against 25 mm allowed.69 For Paris, see building methods.
    • The cost held once the works were let, not before. The second project ended 1% above the ceiling agreed in 2008, but that ceiling was 40% above the estimate put to voters in 2001, in prices five years older.101 257

    Where the comparison stops

    • Size. Each Zürich through station has 4 tracks. Paris Nord-Est would have 20, of which 6 for high-speed trains, 4 for regional express trains and 10 for the two new suburban lines, RER G and RER F; the four Paris stations together, with the new suburban station under Saint-Lazare, would have 48. Zürich is no evidence for a station of that size.
    • The hall stayed. About two thirds of Zürich's long-distance trains still end or turn back in the hall (derived). The Paris project moves every train of Gare du Nord, Gare de l'Est and Montparnasse underground and keeps no surface tracks there; only Gare de Lyon keeps a small surface terminal for suburban line R, and Saint-Lazare its surface station for line J and the Normandy trains. Zürich shows that through platforms relieve a terminus, not that they can replace one.
    • Trains and length. The platforms compare: 420 m in Zürich, 400 m for a double high-speed train in Paris.22 The traffic does not: 140 long-distance trains a day use Löwenstrasse, about nine departures an hour. The pattern tested for Paris has 12 high-speed trains an hour each way running through Nord-Est and 6 more each way on the direct link between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon: see the hour.
    • Depth and price. Löwenstrasse lies 16 m down and was dug from above. In 2026 euros it cost about €0.55 million per metre of platform track (€0.5 to 0.6 million), and that is a final cost. This study uses €1.0 million for the deeper Paris stations, a planning price with 15% risk added on top: see the prices.
    • Stops. Running through did not shorten the stop of trains that wait for connections. A train that turns back in Zürich stands 5 to 12 minutes. In Paris no train is planned to reverse: every high-speed train calls at two of the three stations and runs on. When the lines are full, the 1 train an hour from the south-east left without a partner runs on to the east line as a new link: see the direct link.
    • Time. Nine years from vote to opening for the first station, and fourteen for the second, from the vote of 2001 to the long-distance trains of December 2015.
    The reading

    Zürich supports three claims of this study: through tracks under a terminus add much capacity for their number, they can be built while the station works, and voters will pay for them when the alternative is a worse station further away. It does not support the size, the depth or the cost of the Paris stations, and its long-distance trains gained less time at the platform than one might expect.

    Annex B

    The Elizabeth line: joining two sides of a capital

    London's Elizabeth line is the closest recent case of joining two sides of a capital by a deep tunnel with large stations. It opened in 2022, three and a half years late and 28% over budget. It now carries more than 700,000 trips a day and its fares cover its running cost, yet most of its passengers were already on rail and save a few minutes each. It is also far smaller and simpler than what Paris would need.

    The line and its stations

    Stopping trains from the west used to end at Paddington station, and stopping trains from the east at Liverpool Street station, two terminals at the edge of the centre.269 The project, called Crossrail while it was built, joined them with 21 km of new twin tunnel under central London, one tube for each direction, and added a branch to the south-east.270 The result is one line of more than 100 km and 41 stations, 10 of them new.271 It is run by Transport for London (TfL), the city's transport authority.

    Each mined station has two platform tunnels of about 240 m, and most have a ticket hall at each end, so that one station spans two older ones.277 278 The underground stations have platform screen doors, glass walls between the platform and the track.279 All 41 stations can be used without steps.273

    Journey times before and after

    Paddington to Liverpool Street takes 11 minutes instead of about 20.276 The largest gains are on the new south-east branch, which had no direct railway to the centre. On the older branches the saving is smaller, but the change of train at the terminal disappears. Where the Underground already ran directly, the line saves nothing.

    What the official evaluation measured

    TfL and the national transport ministry published an evaluation of the first two years in 2025.275 It counts perceived minutes: minutes weighted for waiting, crowding and delay, as a passenger feels them.

    A weekday of October 2023TripsMinutes saved per tripMinutes saved in all
    New public transport trips71,0006.3447,000
    Trips already made, anywhere in London6,429,0001.38,552,000
    All trips6,500,0001.48,999,000
    • Small savings for many people. 95% of the minutes saved go to trips that were already being made (derived), including on other lines that became less crowded.
    • Measured from door to door, the typical peak journey between the Paddington area and the Abbey Wood area fell from 74.5 to 45 minutes between 2019 and 2023.275
    • Along the older branches many routes show no significant fall, since trains already ran there. The report gives no minutes for the change of train that disappeared.275
    • The size of the saving that carried London's case is 1.3 perceived minutes a trip across all trips, 6.3 for the new ones;275 this study counts about 2.1 clock minutes a journey for the regional passengers who gain a second stop in Paris, before any weighting: see regional traffic.

    How traffic grew, and where it came from

    The line opened in three steps over twelve months, and traffic rose at each one. Against the last year before the pandemic, yearly journeys have multiplied by 4.3: from 56 million on the two older services to 242 million in 2025/26 (derived).129 130

    Where the passengers came from

    • New trips are about a tenth. The evaluation finds 71,000 more public transport trips a weekday across London, about 1% of the city's total and a tenth of the line's own (derived).275 TfL's first estimate, a year after opening, was twice that (unverified).311
    • The older services kept their traffic; the growth is elsewhere. The traffic that came from them equals about 58 million journeys a year, almost what they carried in 2019/20 (derived).310 129
    • Other lines were relieved. Parallel rail links carry 16% to 22% less than comparable links (derived).275 The line itself has room: in January 2024 it was never above 3 standing passengers per square metre.275

    What multiplied the traffic, and what Paris would have of it

    Three things multiplied the journeys by 4.3. Six new stations were opened in the centre, on a route that had no railway, each spanning two older stations and joined to the Underground. Trains run through instead of ending at Paddington and Liverpool Street, so the change of train at the terminal disappeared. And there are far more trains: 24 an hour through the centre against 15 or 16 into the Liverpool Street terminal before, plus a new branch to the south-east.273 301 The stations of this study give Paris the second of these, and part of the first: the second stop in the centre is a new station for the passenger who used it, though not on a route without rail. They do not give the third. The model runs today's regional express and suburban trains through Paris, with only the extra running that joining the lines needs, and adds no trains; it counts the time saved by the second stop and the journeys that follow from it, at 31.1 million a year, and nothing for more trains, less crowding or journeys across the region. Those are left to study point I14: see what must be verified.

    What this says for a forecast

    Most users of a new through line are people already on rail who save a few minutes. New trips are about a tenth, and the shift from cars is close to nothing. Demand rose 6% to 9% where journeys became 10% shorter.310 This study builds its regional forecast the same way, with an average saving of 2.1 minutes a journey: see regional traffic and the evidence.

    What it cost, who paid, and what came back

    In 2026 euros the final cost is about €32 billion, an order of magnitude converted for this study with British consumer prices and the exchange rate of October 2026.80 313 314 The tunnels were finished in 2015.73 The time was lost afterwards, in the stations and in making trains, signalling and station equipment work together; the delay became apparent only in late 2018.315 Of the last £1.9 billion of cost increase, £0.9 billion was the cost of the delay itself.316

    Who paid

    The supplement on business rates. Business rates are the British tax on business property, charged on the rental value of the premises. Since 2010 London adds 2 pence per pound of that value, the legal maximum, on its larger premises, 13% of them.312 The supplement was to pay £4.1 billion, 28% of the budget of 2010 (derived).294

    The overrun was covered by government loans, most of them to the Greater London Authority, the city's government.316 With a levy on new floorspace paid by developers, the Authority's contribution reached £6.9 billion, 37% of the final funding of £18.8 billion (derived).312 80 It borrowed the money and repays it from the two levies. The supplement is due to end between 2038 and 2041.312

    Fares and running cost

    The line earns more in fares than it costs to run: £177 million more in 2025/26 (derived).130 Two cautions. The surplus is about half of what the Authority pays each year on its loan, and the two sit in different accounts. And at most about half of the income is new to TfL: the rest was already paid on its other lines (derived).310

    For Paris the picture is similar, for another reason. The project keeps no fares of its own, but in the central case of this study the track charges on new high-speed journeys and the charges on new uses cover 189% of the yearly running cost with the whole income package, 164% with the charge on high-speed passengers alone and 134% with no charge at all. Most of it rests on the new traffic across Paris, the least certain figure of the study: see the operations account. How London's supplement serves as a precedent is in the financing precedents.

    Benefits against costs

    A benefit to cost ratio divides what a project is expected to bring, counted in money over 60 years, by what it costs. Above 1, it gives back more than it costs. "Wider benefits" are gains beyond time saved, mainly the extra output of firms and workers brought closer together; they are harder to estimate.

    The same ratio on two bases. British appraisals deduct the fares from the cost before dividing. The 1.97 of 2011 divides the benefits by a cost net of fares of £5.9 billion: capital 9.4, running 3.9, less revenue 7.4, present values in pounds of 2002. User benefits were put at £11.0 billion valued as the national ministry does and £15.5 billion as London does.219 This study divides by the gross cost. On that basis the Elizabeth line stands at about 0.8 with user benefits valued as the national ministry does and 1.2 as London does (derived); this project at 1.17 on gross cost and 1.76 on cost net of its income on its simple reading, and 1.34 under the French rules, which let traffic and the value of time grow: see the comparison.

    What the official evaluation does not show
    • No value for money yet. "It is still too early for an in-depth analysis of the Elizabeth line's value for money."275
    • No result on property or tax. No measured effect on property values or on tax receipts has been published. The figures in circulation, such as "£42 billion added to the economy", are forecasts made by the promoter before the opening.219 218 321
    • Homes and jobs without a cause. 71,000 homes were built within 1 km of stations from 2015 to 2024, and jobs grew, mostly in the City, where the report cannot tell the line's effect apart.131

    What Paris can take from it, and where the comparison stops

    What Paris can take from it

    • The risk is in the stations and the systems, not in the tunnels. Main station contracts tripled or more: Paddington from £181 million to £571 million.102
    • Do not fix the opening date early. The project was "dominated by a fixed completion date" set eight years ahead.315 The official lesson: "Use an evidenced range rather than a single target date."323
    • Fewer contracts, and one body in charge of the joins. With 36 main contracts and nobody but the client managing the joins between them, the client paid for knock-on delays.102
    • Protect the testing period. Trains switch between three signalling systems.102 Preparing the line for service took 14 months against 4 assumed.301
    • Open in stages, and plan the stages again when delay comes.301 For Paris see the stages.
    • Price the stations with care. London's central stations cost €2.0 million per metre of platform track, twice the €1.0 million used here. At the London price the Paris stations would cost about €22 billion more: see the prices used.

    Where the comparison stops

    • London built a large metro. One kind of train, 205 m long. Its 24 trains an hour need only two platform tracks per station. No long-distance train uses the tunnel.
    • Paris would take 400 m high-speed trains. They stand longer at the platform than a metro, so Paris Nord-Est needs 20 tracks, 6 of them for high-speed trains: see how many platforms. Nobody has built a deep station of that size.
    • London joined two suburban networks. Paris would join four high-speed lines, the regional express trains of the north, the east and the Atlantic side, and five suburban lines, merged into two new RER lines (lines H, K and L into RER F, lines P and N into RER G), high-speed and regional express trains in one tunnel and each suburban line in its own, through four stations instead of one line.
    • London had no fast line across its centre; Paris has five. The RER lines already cross Paris, so the gain for each regional passenger is a second stop, not a new railway. That is why the model counts 31.1 million new regional journeys a year on 155 million users, where London multiplied its traffic by four.
    • The cost is larger: €42 billion (€28 to 62 with low and high prices) against about €32 billion, for 2.1 times the tunnel.
    • London's fares pay for running the line. In this study the new income covers 189% of the running cost, 164% with the charge on high-speed passengers alone, most of it from the track charges on new journeys across Paris.
    • A planned frequency is not a promise. The line runs 16 trains an hour at quieter times where its sponsors required 20.304
    The reading

    The Elizabeth line shows that a through tunnel under a capital fills up fast, relieves the lines beside it and can pay for its own running. It also shows that most of the traffic is moved from other lines, and that stations and systems decide cost and delay. Its evaluators warn against carrying the results to other places.275 Zürich, the other precedent, is closer to Paris in kind, with long-distance trains under a working terminal: see Zürich main station.

    Annex C

    The Swiss pulse: every train meets every train

    In Switzerland the timetable was designed first and the works second. Trains from every direction reach the main stations just before the hour and leave just after, so that almost any change takes a few minutes. Lines were made faster only as far as needed to run from one such meeting to the next in under an hour.

    The idea: all the trains are in the station together

    A regular-interval timetable repeats itself every hour: each line leaves at the same minutes all day. The Swiss network has had one since 23 May 1982.324 The pulse adds a second rule. At the main stations, called nodes, the trains of all lines arrive at about the same time and leave again together a few minutes later.325 In the words of SBB, the Swiss federal railway, trains and buses reach a node just before the full and the half hour, or at minutes 15 and 45, and leave shortly after.326 The passenger does not hunt for a connection: it is standing at another platform.

    :45

    Arrivals

      Departures

        Minute, line, place and track for the wave around the full hour. Tracks 31 to 34 are the through platforms under the hall.

        The station's standard minimum for a change is 7 minutes.238 Shorter changes exist where the planner names the pair of trains: Bern to St. Gallen is sold with 4 minutes, because the two trains stand on the two sides of one platform.267 Where no value is set, Swiss timetable data assume 2 minutes.327

        The nodes and the minute at which they beat

        The plan of 1994 named seven nodes. Zürich, Basel, Bern and Winterthur are served at the full hour and, for a large part, at the half hour. Lausanne, Biel and Luzern are served at minutes 15 and 45, because the runs to them are slightly too long for the hour. A node at 15 and 45 needs a train every half hour to give good connections.325

        The 2026 timetable still shows Zürich, Bern and Basel at 00 and 30, and Lausanne and Biel at 15 and 45. Luzern now gathers its trains around the hour, and St. Gallen behaves as a node of its own (derived from the timetable). Choose a station or a line.
