        The plan is the Federal Council's.325 The 2026 columns are derived from the timetable. Passengers per working day in 2023, shown in the panel, are SBB counts.97 Zürich is described by its canton as by far the largest interchange node of the network.343

        Why a run must take just under an hour

        If every train is in Zürich at the hour and every train is in Bern at the hour, a train between the two has just under an hour for the run. The Federal Council put it in one sentence: the concept requires journey times between the nodes of a little under one hour.325 In general the run, with half the stop at each end, must fit a multiple of half the interval: 30, 60 or 90 minutes for an hourly service (unverified).344 Hence the Swiss motto of 1986: not as fast as technically possible, but as quickly as necessary.328

        The same thing on the real board. In 2026 the train from Zürich reaches Bern at :58. The trains to Basel and to Lausanne and Geneva leave at :04, the train to Visp and Brig at :07.345 330 With the 69 minutes of before 2004, it would arrive at :11, after all of them (illustration).

        Where the hour cannot be reached, the node moves. Bern to Lausanne takes 69 minutes, so Lausanne is a node at 15 and 45: the train leaves Bern at :34 and arrives at :43.348 325 Official maps show slots of 60 and 75 minutes on these western lines.349 A target of 57 minutes exists but has not been met,350 and the plan for 2035 assumes 68.351 The western cantons speak of a two-tier network.352

        What it took

        • A vote. On 6 December 1987, 57.0% of voters approved Rail 2000, on a turnout of 47.7%.353
        • A budget that was cut to fit. The credit was CHF 5.4 billion at 1985 prices, about CHF 7.4 billion at 1993 prices. By 1991 the railway's plans would have cost about CHF 16 billion. The first stage was then capped at CHF 7.4 billion.325 Of four new lines in the plan put to voters, one was kept.354
        • One new line. Between Mattstetten and Rothrist, on the way from Bern to Olten: 45 km (47 km in two official papers), for CHF 1.5 billion in the press of 2002 and CHF 1,458 million in the budget of 1994.346 355 326 325 It brought three runs to about one hour at once: Zürich to Bern, Bern to Basel and Bern to Luzern.
        • Trains instead of concrete elsewhere. On the line along the Jura from Lausanne to Zürich through Biel, tilting trains were bought instead of new line. Double-deck coaches gave 40% more seats without longer platforms.325 Works were done only at bottlenecks or where a run between nodes took more than 60 minutes.356
        • The outturn. The first stage opened on 12 December 2004 and cost CHF 5.9 billion, CHF 1.5 billion under its ceiling.355 346

        Three runs came to about one hour with the new line. Three others, in the west, are still 8 to 11 minutes over the hour, and all three are slower than planned in 1994.

        What it gave

        93.2%of trains less than 3 minutes late2024; 94.1% in 202597 364
        98.7%of connections made2022 to 202497

        • The timetable of 2004. 12% more trains and 14% more train-km; about 90% of all times changed.366 Average long-distance journeys became 7% shorter and frequency rose by 20%.367 SBB carried 253.4 million passengers in 2004 and 275.9 million in 2005.368
        • How much is due to the pulse? The official evaluation credits slightly under half of the growth of 1996 to 2005 to the change in service. It judges the coordination of long-distance and regional trains at the nodes a success, but it could not separate the effect of the pulse from that of speed and frequency.365
        • The first step brought nothing at once. The regular-interval timetable of 1982 produced no measurable rise in traffic in its first year.369
        • Protecting it has a price. Since the end of 2024 a badly delayed train is held until the next slot of its pattern, half an hour later, rather than disturb the node.364 For 2025 journey times in western Switzerland were lengthened to keep trains on time and connections safe during works.370
        • A node is greedy in platforms. A station where all trains meet needs more platform tracks than any other pattern.371

        What it would mean for Paris

        An illustration, not a timetable

        What follows shows what a pulse needs and what the through stations would make possible. A sketch of one hour of trains at the three stations, and of what timing them for changes would give, is in the chapter on the timetable. No benefit of a pulse is counted in the model behind this report.

        A pulse needs one thing that Paris lacks: a place where the trains of all lines stand together. Today its main lines end in separate terminals, and a passenger between the north or east of France and the south-east or the Atlantic coast changes stations across the city. In the model this takes 57.5 minutes from train to train. The three through stations do not create one such place either. They are 13 minutes apart by train, a 6-minute run and a 7-minute stop, every high-speed train calls at two of them, and half of the trains of each line pass each station: in the standard hour, 6 of the 12 Atlantic trains run through Nord-Est to the north or the east and 6 take the direct link to Gare de Lyon and the south-east, and the south-east line splits the same way: see which trains pair. A timed meeting would therefore be partial at each station (derived from that pattern). At Nord-Est it could join the north and the east with the Atlantic coast and the south-east, and the north with the east, on the trains that pass there. At Gare de Lyon it could join the south-east with the north and the east, and by the link with the Atlantic coast. At Montparnasse it could join the Atlantic coast with the north, the east and the south-east. A passenger whose train does not call at the right station changes once more, or takes the next train of the hour. A change inside one station is taken as 12.5 clock minutes assumption, and about 47% of the passengers crossing Paris would not change at all, because a train runs through: see crossing Paris.

        A pulse costs platforms. The number of platforms in this report assumes that stops are spread through the hour: 3 high-speed tracks each way at each station, 6 in all, each able to take 5 trains an hour by the rule used, and loaded at 4.3 trains an hour per track at Nord-Est, 5.0 at Montparnasse and 4.0 at Gare de Lyon when the lines are full: see how many platforms. A timetable in which trains meet at fixed minutes would need more tracks, for two reasons. More trains stand in the station at the same moment, and each stands longer: in Zürich a through train that waits for connections stops for 6 to 9 minutes, against 3 minutes for one that does not wait (derived, see Zürich). The other side of the same coin: a pulse station is empty for most of the hour, so its average use, about 6 trains an hour per track at Zürich's Löwenstrasse (derived), is a design choice and not a ceiling. It says nothing about what six Paris tracks could take with stops spread evenly.

        What a pulse at the three stations would ask for

        • The same minutes every hour. The pattern tested in this report has 12 high-speed trains an hour each way running through Nord-Est and 6 on the direct link: see the hour. A pulse would fix the minutes at which they meet.
        • Three beats, not one. A train that meets others at Nord-Est on the hour reaches Gare de Lyon or Montparnasse 13 minutes later, so the southern stations would beat about a quarter of an hour after Nord-Est, and the link trains in between (illustration). Trains from the north and east in just before each beat, trains to the south out just after, and the reverse half an hour later.
        • Platforms known in advance. In Switzerland a line uses the same track hour after hour, and the track is printed weeks ahead (derived).330 Platforms show where each coach stops.62
        • Trains on time. The Swiss pulse rests on more than nine trains in ten arriving within three minutes.97

        Where the Swiss example stops

        • The French timetable is not built this way. High-speed trains do not leave at the same minutes every hour on every line (unverified).
        • Seats are reserved. A Swiss passenger who misses a connection takes the next train half an hour later. A reserved seat is for one train, so a missed connection costs more and the margin must be wider. Today the platform is shown about 20 minutes before departure and access closes 2 minutes before.60
        • Distances are longer. Swiss nodes are about an hour apart, so every train meets a node every hour. On French high-speed lines only the three Paris stations would be such meeting points, and no train calls at all three.
        • Few passengers change. In German long-distance travel 18% of trips include a change between long-distance trains.372 In this study about 5.2 million journeys a year change between Paris stations today, 15.5 million with the new stations.
        • A pulse fills the platforms at the same minute. A station where all trains meet needs the most tracks of any pattern.371 The stations of this report, with 6 high-speed tracks each, are not sized for it.
        The reading

        The through stations are not a pulse, and this report does not need one. They remove what makes a pulse impossible in Paris today: terminals with no train between them. They do not make one meeting point: with three stations 13 minutes apart and every train calling at two of them, a pulse would be three partial meetings. Whether French high-speed trains should then meet at fixed minutes is a choice of timetable that can be made later. It would need regular trains that run on time, and more platforms than the six high-speed tracks a station counted here.

        Annex D

        How the numbers are made

        Enough detail to check the figures or to redo them with better data. Everything is computed by a small open model: Python scripts whose results feed every number in this document, and the same arithmetic in the browser for the calculators.

        The access model

        • Points: 1,000 points on an even grid over Paris, 315 m apart. For the suburbs, the centre of each of 1,265 communes, weighted by population.
        • Network: every metro, RER and tram line, and the suburban train lines for the communes outside Paris, with stations, stop order and published interchange times, from the data of Île-de-France Mobilités of 5 October 2026.86 Buses are not included.
        • Speeds: walking at 4.5 km/h on a path 30% longer than the straight line; each metro line at its own average speed (20 to 28.5 km/h); RER at 60 km/h plus one minute per stop. Waiting is half the interval between trains. In the suburbs, up to 1 km on foot to a station, further at 20 km/h.
        • Result: the quickest time from each point to the hall of each of the four terminals, and to the Nord-Est station taken as the nearer of its two halls.
        • Saint-Lazare is derived, not measured. The network data were not run for Saint-Lazare. For each point and each weighting, a straight line, time = a + b × distance, is fitted on the point's times to Gare du Nord, Gare de l'Est and Montparnasse and applied to its distance to Saint-Lazare. The result is never taken below 6 minutes plus 2.5 minutes a km (a metro at about 24 km/h with access and wait, scaled for the weighting), and walking is used when it is shorter assumption. These times feed only the regional benefits of RER F; they are to be replaced by a run of the network model (study point I22).
        • The triangle's rules: every TGV stops at two of the three stations and no train reverses. Trains to the north and the east stop at Nord-Est and at one southern station; trains between the Atlantic and the south-east stop at Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon by the direct link. Each line keeps its home station, so for each direction the passenger boards at the home station or at the train's other Paris stop.
        • Two measures. The plain one is the time to the entrance of the nearest station where a train of the line stops, the two halves of the trains of each line averaged (27.4 weighted minutes today from Paris, 22.8 with the project). It is the one used to count the benefits of TGV passengers: on a long trip the minutes spent seated on the right train across Paris matter little assumption. The second adds the ride the train then makes between its two Paris stops when the passenger boards at the far one: the 6-minute run between any two of the three stations, the passenger boarding a train already standing at the platform assumption. Crossing Paris keeps the run and the stop, 13 minutes (6 and 7), the beat of the timetable. The second measure supposes that the passenger picks the train of the line that calls at their best station, half of the trains of each line, without a longer wait; it gives 23.2 minutes and is shown on the map and as a case in the accounts. Regional and suburban passengers are counted this way, with their own rides: 7 minutes from Nord-Est to Montparnasse, the same run and a 1-minute stop, and 4 minutes from Nord-Est to Saint-Lazare on RER F assumption.
        • Passenger choice. The central case assumes that passengers take the first train of their line and so get the ride between stops half of the time; the choice measure assumes that they plan around it. The truth lies between the two and depends on frequency and on how tickets are sold assumption (study point I16).
        • Never longer than today: each train still stops where it does now, so no point can lose on either measure; 100% of the Paris points gain and the rest are unchanged. The export script stops with an error if a point loses.
        • Time inside the station is not in these figures. It is compared separately (see inside the station) and tested as two extra minutes for everyone (see the tests).
        • Weights: one run on the clock; one with the official weights on walking, waiting and changing; one with metro and RER riding counted 25% heavier for crowding.

        New passengers are valued at half the time saved, as in every transport appraisal: they gain less than those who already travelled. Yearly figures mix sources that turn a weekday count into a year with factors from 273 to 435, and base years from 2012 to 2025; they are orders of magnitude, not counts. Benefits are held flat over time in the central case; growth of 1.5% a year is a separate case (study point I17).

        Official rules that are not applied. A full French appraisal would let the value of time rise with income, discount at 3.2% to 4.6% instead of 3%,375 and count each euro of public money as 1.2 euros.87 The first helps the project and the other two count against it. The central case applies none of them; growth of benefits and the two discount rates are tested in the tests, and growth is shown beside the flat case in the economic return.

        Cost

        • Build-up. Quantities times unit prices from final costs and signed contracts, which already hold past overruns; the prices, their sources and the test against seven projects are in the cost chapter. Works €28.5bn, then 20% for design and client costs and 7% for land bought, applied to the works; then 15% for risk on the whole, €41.7bn in all (gross-up 1.461).
        • Why 15%. With prices that come from outturns rather than estimates, the allowance covers what is specific to this project and not the general drift of projects, which the prices already contain. The back-test against seven built projects gives the model with 15% a result within the range of the published costs (see the back-test). 10% with low prices and 30% with high prices bound the range: €27.8bn to €62.0bn. Whether reviewers accept 15% is study point I10.
        • The link and the London hall. The direct TGV link between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon is 5 km at the tunnel price; the control hall and waiting room for London departures above Nord-Est are €0.2bn assumption. 4 junctions at €0.25bn, all on the TGV tunnels, and 8 portals and tie-ins at €0.15bn (4 TGV, 2 RER G, 2 RER F) are priced as items.
        • Regional express trains in the TGV tunnels. They have no tunnel of their own. The links that bring them into the TGV tunnels are one item, €0.65bn before add-ons assumption: six tie-ins in the station throats (four at Nord-Est, two at Montparnasse), two dive-unders in the Nord-Est throats where the eastern and Gare de Lyon trains cross the TGV lines, and links at three TGV portal ramps (north, east, Atlantic). The tunnels are planned on paths 2 minutes apart, 30 an hour each way; TGVs keep their places in the 12-minute beat and the regional express trains take the paths between them, every train with the same 6-minute run between stations. This needs signalling for trains about 1.5 minutes apart (ETCS level 2 with short blocks and automatic driving in the tunnels) assumption. Each tunnel's peak load is read against 40 trains an hour if trains can follow 1.5 minutes apart and 30 if 2, against the 75% that planners allow at the peak (UIC leaflet 406). The busiest, the Atlantic approach, is at 65% at 1.5 minutes but would be at 87% at 2. A regional express tunnel to Vanves, 2.8 km, about €0.9bn all-in, is the fallback if signalling only reaches 2 minutes; it is not in the estimate.
        • Tunnels by kind of train. TGVs and regional express trains share one set of twin-track tunnels and each suburban line has its own, priced per km: TGVs 26.8 km (one tunnel on each side of the triangle, the 5 km link and the four approaches), RER G 11.5 km (east approach, Nord-Est to Montparnasse, Atlantic side), RER F 6.2 km (north approach, 2.6 km from Nord-Est to Saint-Lazare with the curve, 1.2 km back to the surface): 44.5 km in all. Corridor lengths are read from maps assumption. The regional transport authority's fee is counted on 39.5 km: the suburban tunnels, 17.7 km, and the 21.8 km of TGV tunnel that the regional express trains use assumption.
        • Stations. 48 platform tracks, 15,300 m in all, priced by the metre: Nord-Est 20 (6 TGV, 4 regional express, 4 RER G, 6 RER F), Montparnasse 14 (6, 4, 4), Gare de Lyon 8 tracks of 400 m (the fourth each way shared by the south-east line's sixteenth TGV and the regional express trains), Saint-Lazare 6 for RER F. Halls are priced at Nord, Est, Lyon and Montparnasse; none at Saint-Lazare, whose surface station stays.
        • Platforms by direction. TGV platforms are dedicated by direction, 3 tracks each way at each station. A stop takes 7 minutes, the track is held 2 minutes more for a late train and needs 3 minutes between a departure and the next arrival, so each train takes a place of 12 minutes and one track takes 5 trains an hour; with the lines full the load is 4.3 at Nord-Est and 5.0 at Montparnasse; at Gare de Lyon it would be 4.0 on three tracks each way, which is why a fourth is added. The three figures of the rule are assumptions (see platforms). Regional express platforms are 350 m, 4 at Nord-Est and 4 at Montparnasse; a 5-minute stop including its margin and a 2-minute gap hold a track 7 minutes a train, against 12 for a TGV. Each way, the regional express tracks at Nord-Est are used 105 of 120 minutes an hour (88%), those at Montparnasse 77 (64%) and the fourth track at Gare de Lyon 40 of 60 (67%). Suburban platforms are 225 m and take 10 trains an hour a track. Both rules are the plan's assumption.

        The two accounts, the return and taxes

        • Yearly repayment. Construction cost, increased by interest during 12 years of even spending, repaid in equal yearly amounts over 60 years at 3% above inflation: each €1 billion costs €43 million a year.
        • Operations account. Costs: running the stations at the rate recorded on the first RER E section (€13,200 a year per metre of platform track) and the tunnels at €2.25 million per km, midway between that record (€3.5 million) and the average of the RER network (€1.0 million); one renewal of the tunnels' rail systems after 30 years, set aside evenly; extra running of regional trains. What today's terminals cost to run is not deducted (study point I11). Income: the TGV charge, the regional express charge, track charges on the new high-speed journeys (two fares for a journey across Paris), new Navigo passes, regional express fares, the authority's fee, shop rents, and half of the operators' saving on trainsets.
        • The TGV charge. It falls only on new uses. A Paris-region passenger pays c for boarding or leaving at a station their line did not serve, and chooses it only when the minutes saved, at €35 an hour, are worth more than c; otherwise they keep their own station at today's price. That choice is made point by point on the access map, and the new journeys follow the time model on the minutes saved less the charge. A passenger who crosses Paris pays 2c; those journeys are multiplied by (1 + 2c / two fares) to the power -0.7, with a fare of €48.50 before VAT.149 A response of -0.5 is shown beside the central one. Track charges are counted on the new journeys, two fares for a crossing assumption. No VAT is counted on the charges.
        • The regional express charge. €2.55 for each passenger who gets off at the second station (22.1 million a year) and €5.10 for each who crosses Paris without stopping (2.8 million), with no loss of journeys counted assumption. Nothing on suburban trains: the Navigo pass and the Île-de-France ticket already cover the ride.
        • Trainsets. With no train waiting in a terminal, operators need 12 to 22 fewer sets at €3 million a set a year; 50% of the midpoint is counted as income in the central case assumption. Shops are counted at half of the Montparnasse yield; full yield is an option shown in the financing chapter.
        • Navigo. New suburban journeys, times the share made by new pass holders, divided by 420 journeys a year per commuter, times the price of a yearly pass.
        • Capital account. The yearly repayment plus any shortfall of operations, less a tax on businesses of the size of the Grand Paris Express one and a European grant; what is left is expressed as a grant paid during the works. No land is sold in the capital account; the parks and the building plots on the terminal sites are valued and costed in the economic return (study point I19).
        • Economic return. Two readings of one list of benefits. The simple reading divides the benefits of the opening year at today's traffic by the yearly cost at 3% over 60 years: passengers' time, the railway's own gains (operators' margin and track charges net of wear), comfort and the regular timetable, job access across Paris, the environment and the parks; new journeys count for half of the gain, and those the charge holds back for none. The official reading applies the French rules: a 4.5% rate, long-distance traffic growing 1.2% a year and values of time 0.8% to 2070, a residual value to 2140, each euro of public money at 1.20, wider effects reported apart; its headline is a net present value. A second ratio divides the benefits by the cost net of the project's income, the basis of British appraisals. The rate of return is the discount rate at which the value is nil.
        • What public budgets get back. VAT at 10% inside the net change in ticket money, less fuel duty on car trips moved to rail. Then three readings of the added activity: none of it is new for the country; or it is counted as in the appraisal the ratios come from (each job worth €10,000 a year of benefits saved, output from denser job markets and from working time saved on the clock taxed at 43.6%); or every job implied is new and taxed on the average output of a job in the region.

        The scripts are in the model folder of the repository: nordest.py (access, traffic, cost), finance.py (accounts, return, taxes), export.py (data for this site). src/js/model.js repeats the accounts in the browser and is checked against the Python results to fifteen digits.

        What has been checked, and what has not

        • Checked by an independent reviewer, on an earlier layout of the project: the access model, the traffic estimates, the construction cost, the two accounts, the passenger charge, the Navigo estimate, what public budgets get back and the comparison with other projects. The figures of the present layout have not been checked again.
        • Not yet reviewed by anyone but their authors: the layout as it stands, with the triangle and its direct link, the tunnels by kind of train, the station under Saint-Lazare, the regional express trains in the TGV tunnels with their paths, loads and links, and the fourth track each way at Gare de Lyon; the platform rules, the regional express charge, the trainset saving, the parks, the second access measure and the derived Saint-Lazare times; and the full count of benefits in the economic return. The study points I1 to I27 listed in risks and next steps are open.
        • Not checked against outside sources by anyone but their authors: the three annexes on Zürich, the Elizabeth line and the Swiss timetable, and the drawings of stations and works, which are sketches.
        • Access times are times to the entrance of a station for TGV passengers, plus the ride between stops for regional and suburban passengers. No minutes are added for the depth of platforms; time inside the station is treated separately.
        Annex E
